utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, Mr. Sivac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm very pleased to be able to start with your evidence today. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, good morning, Excellencies, good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Sivac.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I hope that in e-court we have your book. On page 98 you say that Aziz Aliskovic and his group were to surrender before 1400 hours. They had killed those lads in the car, those reservists and then you continue to say, "I informed them up there at Hambarine to be prepared and to remove the people."

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. Precisely because of the fact that you are misinterpreting some parts of my book, I have the book before me. What did you say, what page was that? 98? Where does it say that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say this, or rather somebody from the Muslim side is explaining what had been said and what the Serbs had requested. The Serbs requested something and then people at Hambarine were informed to be prepared. Who said that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Edo Sadikovic when Mirza Mujadzic and the other from the leadership of the SDA and the HDZ after the takeover of power fled and disappeared from the political scene, the two of them, as respectable and reputable citizens tried to talk to somebody from the Serbian leadership and to delay the start of the shelling of Hambarine. They wanted to prevent innocent casualties among the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You've mentioned Dr. Eso. Is it correct that Dr. Eso authored a text in Kozarski Vjesnik that irritated the Serbs and that that was being done in those critical days in 1992, you said that you liked them but I'm asking you whether those texts were found to be irritating by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we go much further with this process which just follows on to what was happening yesterday, I wonder if we can, since Dr. Karadzic says the book has been uploaded in e-court have the book called up, the relevant page called up and Dr. Karadzic can actually show this Court exactly what passage he's referring to rather than deal with paraphrasing, which -- and allegations of what the witness actually said which no one is in a position to judge without seeing the actual page in front of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I quite agree. What's the e-court number?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D04500. 1D04500.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is your book, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the first edition of my book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's look at page 62. The war has already started in Bosnia --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, just one more thing. I see that there is now a document in English on the screen in front of you, and just to avoid any misunderstanding about the nature of this document, that English document is not a translation, it doesn't purport to be a translation. As far as we are able to see, it's some kind of topical summary of some 58 pages of this book of more than 250 pages that may be more of a guide to what the book might contain, but not having the translation, I'm not prepared to say to Your Honours that this summary is even accurate. So I just want to make that abundantly clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, can you help us in this regard?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that these are excerpts, translated into English, but not in the right order. You can see that the book is actually a diary, and the translation was done by the Prosecution. They have selected the parts to be translated, and I don't think that they paraphrased. I believe that the text was translated word for word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I just said that it was not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I see the ERN number.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I can be helpful so the Court can see it very quickly, if you look at the last passage on the first page it says the author describes, the author comments on. You can see on its face, it doesn't pretend to be a translation. It's sort of a topical guide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My question is, who prepared this? Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, it is an OTP product which is another reason why we can say with some confidence it's not a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you concede that it is prepared by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, but it is not a translation of what the witness has written. It's a guide to what the contents may be. In other words, generally speaking, what topics or issues are addressed at particular areas so ... I think Ms. Edgerton's point was that - and I hope it's been useful - was that the Court not be misled into thinking that this is a translation of what the witness's words are in the book. Instead, it's a description by someone who reviewed the book about what that person considered some of the passages contained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That's helpful. We can proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, if the witness is here, I believe that he can confirm for us or deny what his book says. We are really not responsible for this English version. I would like to call up page 62 in the book. In e-court it has to be a different page. It's 59 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here you say that Milosevic is shooting at Sarajevo according to Kozarski Vjesnik. There is war going on in Sarajevo but Kozarski Vjesnik is a Muslim and Serbian paper.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the same texts were published by Kozarski Vjesnik at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now can we look at page 67 in the book? 64 in e-court. Is it true that you observed some renegade gangs in Prijedor and that you wrote about that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those were individuals with criminal past who had arrived from Serbia and ended up in Prijedor. They made most of the time of lack of law and order to instigate incidents, to enter Muslim houses and to loot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please read the first sentence in the second paragraph from the top of the page?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, you, if you can, just the first sentence.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Different groups of thugs started" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note we do not have that on the screen and the witness is reading too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The interpreters were not able to follow. What paragraph did you refer to? And when you -- when reading, Mr. Sivac, could you slow down for the benefits of the interpreters? Do we have that passage in front of us?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Serbian, it is the second paragraph on the page starting from the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, we don't have to go on. However, you don't say here that they were from Serbia but just that they were gangs and that nobody could do anything to them.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, everybody knew where they had come from. It was self-understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You go on to say that a lad beat up an officer, he was remanded in custody by the army and then released very soon thereafter, and then he went and joined Slavko Ecimovic in the forest; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I wrote about that event.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you wonder how come that the military had become so humanitarian in nature and that they didn't keep him for a long time?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That young man was well known to all security services. He had a criminal record. He had just arrived from one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What page are we referring to? As far as I can see it's not on the pages on the screen in front of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The book is not evidence. And then we don't have English page. Does it have any point of having a specific page? That's why I let him go. And the witness confirmed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Keep in mind this book is not in evidence. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we can tender the pages from which we quoted and which the witness confirmed but I don't have the time to quote but if the witness confirms --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you are minded to tender the pages you showed to the witness, then you have to upload the correct page so that we can follow.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we then look at page 78 in the book? I believe it's 74 in e-court. Just bear with me. 75 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say that you are standing on the banks of the Sana with your cousin or nephew, and you ask him, "Did you return your rifle and uniform you were a member of the reserve police?" I asked Adnan. "I didn't and I won't because I will still need it." Is that what he told you?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the page be admitted can the book be given an exhibit number and can the page be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What page? Do you mean page 78?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. 75 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be assigned Exhibit D1742 marked for identification. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then it says a lull before the storm. And there you describe how you gather spontaneously in various pubs and bars and you discuss the situation, you and your friends; right?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's on the same page. So it can stay as is. And now can we look at page 80? 77 in e-court. In May you spoke to Dr. Eso and he says: [As read] "Our party leaders who instigated people the most fled and left the people in the cold, and the only person who stayed behind is the president of the municipality." Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, more or less.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this page be admitted and can we go to the next one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That can be added. Page 80 in hard copy.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just bear with me for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Eso smiled and said that he had visited Slavko at Kurevo. He found about 100 lads there. They are not well-armed. They need weapons and food. This is still on page 81, the fourth passage from the top right. He informed you that he had visited Slavko at Kurevo, Slavko had about 100 lads, he needed weapons, food and tobacco. He would go there again and he asked you to prepare things for him. Is that what he said?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So Dr. Eso is not only a charmer but he is also Slavko Ecimovic's logistics man?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was Slavko Ecimovic's friend and it says on one of the pages of my book that he was the one who tried to dissuade Slavko from embarking on any adventures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, it says here that you should prepare food and weapons, that he would go and visit Slavko at Kurevo again. What is Kurevo?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kurevo is in the hinterland of Hambarine, in Prijedor, but Eso said it in very general terms, not only to me, there were a few other friends of mine together with me there and he -- when he said, "You should ...," he meant all of us, plural.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So he says you have to prepare something to -- for me to take to them. He -- they are up there, they decided to fight, please prepare something. Is that what it says here?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that was taken out of the context. Slavko Ecimovic did not intend to fight in Prijedor. They intended to join the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and to try and break through to the Bihac territory and there they were going to join the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did they not attack Prijedor after that instead of going to Bihac? Am I right in thinking that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, in my statement or rather on day 1 of my testimony I told you that there were a lot of contradictions there. You gave me a list of those potential or possible attackers who had attacked this town of Prijedor. Among them are the names of some individuals who most probably according to what I know and especially remember after such a long time, simply convinced Slavko Ecimovic to embark on that adventure, but the underlining idea was to break up the group.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So those Muslims were working on behalf of the Serbs, they trapped Slavko?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and last time when we spoke, you told us that you received information on the same day as to what the Muslims had been up to. The same situation prevailed among those who were in Slavko's group. There were people there who from day 1 participated in fighting in Croatia in the most elite Serb units there. And they were even decorated as good fighters. And now look at the excerpt: They went to Slavko and they convinced him that they should go and liberate Prijedor in other words, those Serb heroes were out there, apparently, to fight against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Serb heroes of Muslim faith; right?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. If you want me to, I can mention their names, but I don't think it's necessary. You will find their names on the list that the security services of Prijedor submitted to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then grateful Serbs reported all those men of theirs in Slavko's unit to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is the biggest farce in all of that. I mean even you are coming to the fact that something is not quite right here. These people were freed in some sort of staged procedure. They survived but they were not in the camp. They went through all of these traumas that they went through, and now are in some other countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, some other witnesses will confirm that. Mr. Sivac, on page 90, I think this is page 87 in the e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I wonder if we could remove the English version from the right-hand side of the page so we could just have the whole B/C/S page displayed. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please look to check if it's correct that Croat Branko Bijekic, the commander of the Ljubija police station was replaced by Aliskovic and the others because he was not in favour of the fighting? Can you look at what it says here, how to install Serbian power and so on and so forth and that is thus I will tell you which paragraph that is, that is the last paragraph, the biggest paragraph, the duties of the commander here were performed by Croat Branko Bijekic, he was probably their man who tried to implement what the SDS leaders and security services of Prijedor asked him to do. What was it that they asked him to do, what did the SDS ask him to do? Not to fight?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the SDS. Would you like me to read it so that the interpreters can -- but I think that the Trial Chamber has an English version. You can see that I do not mention fighting anywhere. I am only saying that the Serbian authorities in Prijedor were prevented --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Approach to Ljubija and Kozarac and Muslim concentrations?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It's not like that. You're paraphrasing again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. You tell us how it was?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Branko Bijekic was the police commander who completely listened to the Serbian authorities, which had come to Prijedor by force and he tried to join that police station too, to the Serbian police station in Prijedor. However, a group headed by Aziz Aliskovic opposed that, also Fikret Sarajlic and others, and they simply forbade Branko Bijekic from coming to the Ljubija police station, and as the people of Kozarac, they accepted that the police station in Ljubija bear the insignia or markings of internationally recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that the same Aliskovic who was charged with the murder or the killing of a soldier in Hambarine? There are two Aziz Aliskovics or is this the same person?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the same person. However, on 22 May the Ljubija police station was taken over by the new Serbian authorities, and all the policemen who were Muslims and Croats were driven away from their posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And were they authorised to replace him or was this a lynch?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, lynch is a strong word, but I don't know what to say for what was done in Prijedor when the Serbian Democratic Party with the help of the army and the police actually perpetrated a much greater lynch.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we adopt this page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. This will be added.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 99, please? And that is probably 97 in e-court. 96, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I ask you where it says here: [As read] "We reached Kurevo, one of the defenders testified, we came from Kurevo to Hambarine, and engaged into battle in order to protect the people. In this direct battle, we killed a number of Chetniks this was our first action and our first fight"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says here. This is paraphrasing. It's something that one of those young men from up in Hambarine said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you can see there that some zoljas were broken down. Who said this, do you know?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that his name is the same as yours, his name is Senad Karadzic, the son of Ferid Karadzic, who was killed down there on the left bank of the Sana.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And can you look at what you say underneath Kozarac? The people of Kozarac had a reputation of being well-armed and well-trained and that they would not surrender so easily; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is my own interpretation and my own impressions based on what I heard and what I read in the Kozarski Vjesnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And that is why you say that is why the Serbian people postponed resolving the question of Kozarac and the neighbouring settlements?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So the question is: Did the Serbian authorities postpone and did they negotiate during that time?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you this, already in 1992 Simo Drljaca and the Serbian authorities kept waving and showing some lists which were -- did not actually show that the people of Kozarac were well-armed, that they had 3.500 rifles and weapons, none of that was actually true. This was just their way of motivating the Serbs to create a sense of mistrust among them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we adopt this page, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the following page, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now here you describe the 24th of May. This is all after Hambarine; is that right, when the Serbs issued an ultimatum for the weapons to be handed over and to have Aliskovic and those killers responsible for the shooting on those soldiers to surrender, and then you say on the third and fourth paragraph from the top the weapons that came into Kozarac and were distributed to the people were there thanks to able individuals, people who loved their country, rather than the result of work of some organisations and powers and parties that were in power. Among those who obtained some weapons were Hasan Didin, Omer Mahmuljin, Kole Kusuran, Azur Jakupovic, Captain Sead Cirkin and so on. And then you say Becir Medunjanin, Mustafa Tadzic, Islam Bahonjic, bravely stood up, young men who entered into legend and on whom Kozarac will be proud of, Hasan Mujcic, Didin; Suad Besic, Dudo; Sejo Bahonjic; Muamer Kulenovic; Dado Blazevic and others. And then you continue with some more names. So these are people who had embarked into battle against the Serbian military and you declare them heroes; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. When I read this text, yes, but don't forget, Mr. Karadzic, that they were the legal representatives and they had the right to fight and they had the legal right to defend their homes. They were members of the regular police of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So don't forget that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. I hope that we will have a little more time because the schedule has been changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, don't rely on that. The Chamber at the moment is not minded to extend your time for your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we tender this page, please? Then I will be under time pressure. And the interpreters are going to complain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, this will be added.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the document 65 ter 05748 and then we will go back to the book again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You agree that from 6 April until 24 May, Kozarac was not touched and it was not touched until the incident in Hambarine; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please look at this document?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a report, military secret, strictly confidential, and so on and so forth, command of the 1st Krajina Corps describing the liquidation of the Green Berets in the broader area of Kozarac on 27 May. So the battle for Kozarac lasted for three days; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The shelling lasted for a day and a half, and then the Serbian infantry, their elite units, took a very short time to overrun Kozarac and the broader area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you look at points 3 and 4, where there is a reference to 1.500 to 2.000 men without heavy weapons and it indicates the areas.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic please be asked to repeat the name?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Could you repeat the name? Interpreters couldn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 4, there is a description of where the Green Berets were deployed, and it refers to the names of these localities, and then it states that there were between 80 and 100 persons killed and about 1.500 captured, and it states that a number of the Green Berets, 100 to 200 persons, were at large on mount Kozarac, among the Serbs there were five killed and 20 wounded. Minor damage on the track assembly of two M-84s and so on and so forth. Do you agree that there were 80 to 100 killed and about 1.500 captured?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I do not agree with that, Mr. Karadzic. According to my information, when Kozarac was ethnically cleansed about 800 people of Kozarac were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's take it slowly. We will come to that. So this is from that time, it's a strictly confidential military report on a completed action.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we tender this, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The witness didn't agree with the document or the contents of the document, but I have no issue with the authenticity of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And assigned Exhibit number D1743. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we go back to the book now again, the previous document? Can we look at page 104 in the book? In the e-court, that is page 101.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you look at the bottom of the page, 27 May, could you please read out to us these last four lines at the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is real chaos today in Prijedor. Expelled persons from the area of Kozarac are arriving from all sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So the persons who are expelled from Kozarac are arriving to the town where the Serbs are in a majority; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They just came for a short period of time, and then would be assembled by the Serb police into trucks and taken to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Well anyway, they are fleeing to Prijedor. Can we look at the next page, please? And can we tender this page, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Adding it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When I asked you if you were told that Keraterm was a temporary shelter, you said that nobody said that. Can you look at the second paragraph from the top, the Serbian authorities explained that Keraterm was just temporary accommodation until the combat quiets down; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what you say but Keraterm was not temporary accommodation. It was there until 6 August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you not write that the Serbian authorities explained that Keraterm was a temporary accommodation?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it says that but this is a lie. It's an outrageous lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we just look at this? You say that dugouts are referred to in Kozarusa and that a radio station was found and you said that these rumours contributed to the preparation of the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. I quoted an extremist Serb here who was sending out false news items about a person from Kozarac whom we all knew very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were there dugouts around Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It is not correct that there were dugouts around Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you we will come to that but perhaps not with you but we have Muslim sources about that. Can we tender this page, please, and then can we go to page 107?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 105 will be added.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, can I make a quick observation? I know Dr. Karadzic feels he's moving fast but he challenges the witness based on something allegedly said, that is the -- whether Keraterm was a temporary facility and then asserts that the witness said that before. In fact, I struggled to find any previous reference along those lines, and the question was, do you remember that you were told that you would be in Keraterm or rather in Omarska for only a short period of time, that you would be interviewed and that you would then be sent home. So what the witness was directly told when he went to, in that case, Omarska was changed which Dr. Karadzic then transmutes later to assert that the witness is changing his testimony, which is obviously not the case. That is one reason why we have attempted to insist in the past upon the transcript references for such representations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. However, the Chamber is able to follow. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we see if this is correct: It says that several groups of brave Kozarac defenders did withdraw and decided and opted for guerrilla warfare. Now, if you look further, page 107 at the bottom, the last paragraph: [As read] "Several groups of brave Kozarac defenders decided after all to withdraw to the Kozara woods and opted for a guerrilla warfare and trying a breakthrough through the forest towards the river Una"; correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's what it says there, that's the information pertaining to 28 May 1992 but it comes from other sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you know that such groups as this one actually stayed in the Prijedor area up until 1994 occasionally killing villagers who -- farmers who were working the land and attacking patrols?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what you're saying, Mr. Karadzic. But I don't have that information and I don't believe it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender this, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, on this page, would you agree, you describe what the Main Board of the SDA did, that they dispersed, that they were irresponsible and so on, and then in the penultimate paragraph you say: [As read] "However, in spite of all these things that they failed to do at the time, this all will be resolved toward the end of the war." And then you mention: [As read] "Mirza Mujadzic, Hilmo Kopovac [phoen], Emir Mujadzic, Denijal Dzafic, Elvedin Rizvanovic, Nijaz Kapetanovic, Mustafa Keric and others will have to face those who remained alive and who went through the hell of Hambarine, Kozarac, Prijedor, Brdo, Keraterm, Omarska ..." and so on. So --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please repeat the last part of his question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac. The interpreters were not able to hear the last part of your question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I asked this: You feel that they are responsible. For what? What is their responsibility, according to you? And the witness was actually on his way to reply.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because with their Serb friends, they escaped and they were safe and they left the people, the civilians, there at the will of the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sivac, did you know that in various variants that we adopted, Prijedor was envisaged, the entire area of Prijedor, or some of the Muslim areas, to be part of a Muslim republic?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what you're saying today, but me and my folks from Prijedor, we never heard of any such proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now have page 112? I believe that's page 109 or 110 in e-court but it's page 112 from the book -- 109 in e-court. An attempt to liberate, can you see toward the end, does it say here in the morning around 400 -- 4.20 fire broke -- there was a lot of firing, there was a lot of shooting on the street before that as well. They were just trying to celebrate and shooting in the air. They would come to the main street and then empty their magazines, but this morning, however, it seemed to be a bit serious. The shooting was getting more serious. And it was approaching the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And that's what you said there?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We supposed that there was fighting going on, and that there were only a small arms used.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the attack that was led by Slavko Ecimovic, an attack on Prijedor; correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you say an attack but what I'm saying is that was an attempt to liberate Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we tender this page, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 112 will be added. Mr. Karadzic, we will be adding those pages that have been referred to by you only.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that suits me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So it is your intention not to tender page 108?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have it, Your Excellency, but it slipped my mind. What I would like to tender is the documents or the pages that I'm asking for here, and that I'm trying to check with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where he says his Serb friends, Mujadzic and others. Can we now have 123, page 123, please, that's page 120 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here you explain what the Serb newspapers reported on but before that there is your note, your comment: [As read] "There was no doubt any more, Prijedor had been attacked, and the citizens were trying to get closer to the centre of the town because they saw the Green Berets withdrawing"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, but there was what the Serb papers reported and I'm just quoting that part of their reports, newspaper reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You're quoting that a little lower but you're not saying that this is a quote as well. These are your words?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, Mr. Karadzic. Would you please take a look at the subtitle there? It is in bold print. It says, "What the Serb newspapers reported on the attack on Prijedor." And then it goes on to say there was no doubt any more, everyone knew that Prijedor had been -- is being attacked and the citizens of the downtown areas because they saw the Green Berets withdrawing close to the reserve officers' hall knew that the Serbs had managed to defend Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But look at the third paragraph, it says although this task was relatively easy, well, would Serbs actually use this term "lahak" for "easy"? Or is that a Muslim variant of the word "lak" in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Serbs wouldn't use this but actually, the person who revised the text, this text, just decided to use the Bosniak term.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we please tender this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 128, please? I believe in e-court that's 125.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mention Mirzet and you say that -- or actually, he writes something here. You actually quote his words. Is this correct, what he states here?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for the most part it is correct. I paraphrased his words or I paraphrased his words in a conversation he had with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That Slavko had managed to obtain some zoljas and other weapons and that the entire areas of Carakovo, Hambarine, Rizvanovici, Rakovcani, Biscani and Sredici were still free territory so that in those areas we were able to organise free movement; correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But that was up -- that was before 20 July when the ethnic cleansing of these parts of the Muslim -- of the Prijedor municipality began.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, would you please refrain from comments? Now, I will put questions to you and you just answer them. Can we have the next page, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The witness was, quite properly, contextualising his answer for the benefit of everyone in the courtroom and not making any comments. It's not, with respect, for Dr. Karadzic to admonish the witness in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Sivac, do you know that at one point, there was an intermingling of the fighters and the civilians, those who actually were combatants, they mingled with civilians, and on 3 May over 3.000 people were arrested?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I've already asked you earlier to mention the time and site or locality that you're referring to when you put a question to me. I don't understand what you're referring to here, what area and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Sivac, I'm talking about the attack on Prijedor, or as you put it, the attempt to liberate Prijedor, which occurred on 30 May. Now, is it true that a lot of civilians from combat-affected areas had actually arrived or been trickling into Prijedor and is it true that at that time, over 3.000 people were taken prisoner, they were all intermingled there, the combatants and the civilians, they were taken prisoner, and taken to Keraterm, correct, and then from Keraterm to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, after this operation, this attempt at liberating Prijedor, within two hours, Slavko Ecimovic's group was completely broken up and most of the men of his men were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's not what I'm asking you about. I'm asking you, as I put it already: Did a lot of civilians congregate on Prijedor or were over 3.000 people arrested and taken to these two centres that I mentioned earlier?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, your question is not clear. What do you mean people congregated on Prijedor? What do you mean by "congregated"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what you said. You said that people fled Kozarac and went to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we've already cleared that up a few moments ago and I explained what exactly I was referring to, but now you're talking about Prijedor. The people from Kozarac have nothing to do with the people from Prijedor. Would you please keep them separate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did civilians from Kozarac flee to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, you are going on and on with the same story. I already told you a few moments ago that, yes, a group of civilians from Kozarac did -- or were -- did arrive but then they were rounded up, put on buses and sent to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, that was the case with those people who were -- who -- for whom it was impossible to find any accommodation - right? - but the others were put up with their friends.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, but that only lasted a couple of days but then the police went and also rounded up those people, put them on buses and sent them also to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you were taken into custody on 10 June and then you were sent back home because it was an error, correct, and then and you writes about there on page 156, probably 153 in e-court, and then you were stopped and those escorts who were taking you back home just barely managed to actually save you from those people who were on the road and who intercepted the vehicle. Well, these people who escorted you that were in the car with you they got out of the car they actually bribed those attackers with some cigarettes and then they saw you off home?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his question [sic]?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think we've completely missed the witness's answer because of the speed at which Dr. Karadzic has been moving.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think the witness said that's correct. Is it correct, Mr. Sivac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yeah, well, what I said was that Mr. Karadzic is trying to actually blend together the people of Kozarac and the people of Prijedor but they have nothing to do, one with the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, we are talking about the check-point here, Mr. Sivac, and we are talking about your escorts. They got out of the vehicle, they bribed those attackers with cigarettes, and then they escorted you home; correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. What you've just mentioned now, that's correct. I described that in my book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the second occasion, it was on 20 June, you were arrested again and this time you were told that it was not an error; correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you ever find out, on the basis of whose interrogation or, rather, stories, were you arrested the second time around and when they said that it wasn't an error?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they never mentioned why or on whose authority they arrested people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not asking you about on whose authority. I'm asking you about the following: After they questioned some other people they concluded that they should arrest you again. Now, who was it who actually said things about you that led to your arrest? Based on whose testimony or based on whose statement were you arrested the second time?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were no statements or no interviews. What are you trying to say? People were just picked up in the street, if they ran into a Serb patrol, they would just be picked up, if they were recognised as Muslims, they would be picked up, taken to -- into custody and taken to Keraterm or Omarska, depending on where.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But didn't they find out that, together with Dr. Eso and others, you actually supplied Slavko and his renegade group with logistics, logistical materials? That's what you also mention in your book; correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, you're trying to impute things to me that I did not say. Mr. Karadzic, I don't want to use a profanity because I respect this Court but -- in my answer to you, but let me just say that this is one of the most stupid things I ever heard in my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you told us about the destiny of a man named Crnalic; correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, his name was - and let me just make very clear - Asmir, Vico, Crnalic, he's a neighbour of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But is there any difference between what really happened to him and what you wrote about in your book?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no I don't see any difference. He was a participant and a victim in that incident and I described the way that incident occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us briefly what it was that happened to him, what was it that you saw?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I saw a part of what happened, and I also learned from some other people who were in the immediate vicinity of the incident, whether Asmir, Vico, Crnalic was killed and I already talked about this person at length. This is a young man who was retarded from an early age, and I don't know, according to you who would have said anything about him that would give grounds for his being taken into a camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, if we had more time, I would go into details but would you please describe what it was that you saw yourself?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I saw, and as I said I also heard from the people who were in his immediate vicinity, that at one point, he was very thirsty and he got to his feet, he raised a bottle, trying to signal the guard that he needed water, and that he would like to go and pour some water into the bottle. The guard did not allow him to do that. He just pretended like he was drinking from that bottle, and then he began to dance, he did a jig, and then a group of guards surrounded him because they didn't know that he was a retarded man, and at one point they even encouraged him, they started telling him, "Come on, come on, keep on going." And then one of the most bloodthirsty of those guards who co-ordinated the work of the interrogators and the people who arrested these detainees, and then he, Asmir Crnalic, ran out of that building and he was taken to the "White House". He was taken to the room of the left-hand side which was really meant for execution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How do you know that, sir?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know, Mr. Karadzic, because whoever ended up in that room was killed in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What did you see? Which of the killings, which of the executions did you see?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, this is a very hypocritical question. Are you saying that we could take photos, that we actually gloated in the murders that were carried out by your subjects?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, you are an eyewitness, you're a participant, a protagonist, a victim. What did you see?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw at first -- when Asmir, Vico, Crnalic was trying to leave the "White House" through a window and to go back to where all of us were, and when he put his foot on the windowsill, one of the guards who was standing guard, the sentry near the restaurant, shot at him and at that moment, we received a command to lie down with -- facing the asphalt road, and then we were allowed to sit up again after a while, and then we saw Asmir Crnalic's dead body lying motionless in front of the "White House".

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In 1D05 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can Mr. Karadzic repeat the document number?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the Kvocka case you said that he started spitting water on them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 1D04501? Page 4093.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you have seven minutes to conclude.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say this: He started spitting water on them and then you say that you didn't see him jumping out of the window. And you didn't say that. And today you're saying that you actually saw that.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you didn't specify who he spit water -- who he spat water at. Previously I was asked whether he was spitting water at the guards and that's not true because they were at a distance from us inmates.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the direction of the guards, can you see that, in the direction of the guards?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. That's a wrong interpretation. The guards were at some distance of at least ten metres from us. He was spitting water on the asphalt.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then you say that you didn't see him jumping out of the window; right?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that we had to lie down facing the asphalt and that I heard some of the things from those people who were closest to the "White House." That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In line 22, in line 20 you were asked did he jump out the window and you say, I didn't see it, and I didn't say that. Is that right? Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that. I don't know what it says here, but I have just given you the complete story surrounding Asmir's murder. You asked me whether I saw any of the executions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we now look at the amalgamated statement, page 179? You speak about similar things. However, you say that he was spitting water towards them and that he jumped out of the building through the building and then that the guard opened fire at him?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible, Mr. Karadzic, that was my first statement in 1994. I gave it to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The amalgamated statement, page 179, that's what I'm reading from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm afraid there is no amalgamated statement in this case.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The material that was tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Which of the executions of killings did you see, Mr. Sivac, which of them at all?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I saw the killing of Asmir Crnalic, Vico. I also --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Let me just ask you this: After that, they came and asked you what his name was and they made a note of that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't come to me. The shift leader asked who knew the man and I just happened to be nearby and I gave them his name and the name was confirmed by the neighbours from his street who were together with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Your Excellencies, please give me the minutes leading up to the break. I need one last question and three sub-questions. In the Stakic case, you said that he managed to jump through the window - right? - that's in the Stakic case page 174 in the amalgamated statement or rather in the material that was proffered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is tendered is his testimony in Stakic case. Not an amalgamated statement or of that sort.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's instead of the amalgamated statement according to 92 ter. That's what I meant. So far we had amalgamated statements and this is instead of. 22700, I think that's the 65 ter number and the page number is 6728 through 6733 and you're describing the event and you say that he managed to jump through a window and that later on you could infer or conclude that he had been killed; right? That's page 174 in e-court and the document has been admitted according to 92 ter rule. You were lying on your stomach and later on you could conclude or rather you say, "We were able to confirm that he had indeed been killed." Right?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And what is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that he had jumped out of the window, that he had escaped the "White House," and that he was killed by the rifle shots?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. You're misinterpreting my words again. When we saw the dead body of Asmir Crnalic in front of the "White House," people who were lying on the road were closer to the "White House" and they told us that he had put his foot on the windowsill in order to jump out of the room where he had been locked in and then when he was on the windowsill he was shot at and killed and obviously his body fell out of the building in front of the window.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now you are quoted as saying: [As read] [In English] "Asmir Crnalic was trying to jump out of the window and that he had managed to jump out of the window. And then the guards shot him. Is this correct, what you stated in your statement?" [Interpretation] And you say that you were very emotional and that that was your 1994 statement, that you adhere by your words, your memory was fresh at the time; isn't that what you said?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where can we find that passage?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I can find is over the course of a number of pages actually, and the last couple of sentences of Dr. Karadzic are pulled from page 6733 of the trial transcript in the Stakic case and I would submit are actually put out of context again to this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I had enough time, I would take things at a time and then we would be better off. Page 179 in e-court, both question and the answer. Everything is there. I quoted the question and that's a quote from the statement as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's upload that page. Yes, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President, a quick translation issue at 32:15, I heard the witness use in his language the word "pista" it was translated as "road." "Pista" is a particular -- has been used repeatedly as a particular area of Omarska camp and it was often referred to by that name so I think that can be checked in the -- on the original tape and probably should be.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter confirms that the witness, indeed, used the word "pista."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And this is the wrong trial proceedings. That's because Dr. Karadzic didn't give the right 65 ter number to my colleagues. I think that you are looking for 22701A.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. 22701A, I believe that now we have it. There was a mistake but not mine. And now I believe we have the right page. This is the page, right. Line 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's just look at the question. Bear with me. And your question -- your answer starts on page 17. Or rather in line 17. And let me read for you. [In English] [As read] "Let me tell you, sir, when I recount this event I sometimes become emotional perhaps, but I abide by my first statement because in 1994 my memory was fresher and I remembered more details. I see now that these details are very important to you. The essence is true. Asmir, Vico, was a sick man. He was taken to the "White House." When he tried to escape from the "White House" to the "pista," he was shot." [Interpretation] And so on and so forth. Is that what you stated? Was that your evidence? Right or not?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What right or not? What was your question? I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have just read out your answer back to you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What else did you see? Who else was killed?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, in Omarska, there were a lot of killings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me just about those that you saw, that you testified to.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to understand that we were not there on some kind of a holiday or a seminar of some sort, that we were able to debate things or observe what was going on. Your most important strategy was --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you, just tell me what you saw.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw people who were dying from beatings and torture, that they had been subject to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Tell us that. What did you see?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Come to your last question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can 1D0500 be admitted? Page 16 in e-court. We saw it the day before yesterday. Then also page 68, 34.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The pages shown to the witness can be added in consultation with the Prosecution. Yes, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think Dr. Karadzic is referring to pages that were shown the day before yesterday to the witness, and there actually were no pages shown the day before yesterday to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's why I referred to the consultation. So with the confirmation from the Prosecution, those pages shown to the witness can be checked and then later added to that exhibit. Do you see some problems?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I do see some problems but -- because there was nothing shown to the witness, and in the spirits of fairness, the witness, and in fact nobody in the Chamber, were in the position to find out whether the witness was accurately quoted to understand any context, to what was discussed with him. All we had was paraphrased and the witness dealt with that as best he could. All that being said, what we could try and do is engage in discussion with the Defence and perhaps having said over these matters and perhaps having said that, the Prosecution might want to reserve the right to review those pages and pages around them and perhaps add relevant portions for the proper context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Of course. We do appreciate your understanding. Come back to the Chamber if there is a problem. But your last question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I respond briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No need. You don't have to. I take it you concluded?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I will wrap it up. I announced a question with three sub-questions, that was going to be my last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, Mr. Sivac, that in Serbia there are around 68 to 70 per cent Serbs and there are 30 per cent non-Serbs, Hungarians, Bulgarians, the Roma, Czech, Poles and so on and so forth? Do you agree or do you know that fact, that there are about 30 per cent of national minorities residing in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with statistical data but I don't have the reason not to believe you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you read the Islamic Declaration?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I read only classics, Mesa Selimovic, Ivo Andric, Garcia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, that's very commendable. Let's now look at page 64 in your book. I believe it's 61 in e-court. 04500. Page 61 in e-court. 1D04500. That's it. And now can we look at page 61, at least I believe it's 61. No, no, this is a good page. Can I ask you to read the intentions of the leadership of the SDA in this paragraph here?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What paragraph, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Read all of it. Starting with the intentions of the leadership. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness be asked to read slowly in order to be interpreted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you start again and slow down when reading, Mr. Sivac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [As read] "The intentions of the leadership of the Party of Democratic Action in Prijedor may have been honest and correct, but in a duel with the Serbs they were losing, wasting time and losing battles, because you can play fair only if the other players play fair. However, on the opposing side there were those who openly said there is no co-existence and peace between the Orthodox faith and other peoples and their institutions. That's why the Serbs will make it their right to use force and military to arrange their own world where the Orthodox faith will prevail and where only Serbs will live."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic start his question all over again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Start again your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at the sentence, "there is no peace and question existence between the Orthodox faith and other peoples and their institutions." Wasn't that the principal maxim of the Islamic Declaration? Or is that the maxim of the Serbian people who have 30 per cent of the national minority living with them? Why did you copy this from the Islamic Declaration, Mr. Sivac?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are your words, Mr. Karadzic. You are saying this. As an author and as a man who wrote a book, I had every right to use poetic licence and to use various sources and to quote things that at that moment I deemed to be the most important for me and for the book. I wanted to use the best expressions in order to best qualify all those things that were happening in the territory of the municipality of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the transcript we have poetic licence however, you said what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The record does not show what is the answer and what is the question. We come -- should come to an end. Do you have any redirect examination, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then your final question, on an exceptional basis, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question was this: You're here testifying under oath. You are not a writer. So there is no licence either for me or for you. Are you claiming that what you wrote in the book refers to the Serbs or is it rather the principal postulate of the Islamic Declaration of Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't read the Islamic Declaration written by Alija Izetbegovic. However, the statement that I included in my book is correct and I'm saying this under oath. Whatever I wrote in my book I still adhere by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And my final question: Of all the former Yugoslav republics which of the republics had more minorities than Serbia and the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, he's had his final question. That's final plus one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That's it, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can these pages be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 64 will be added to the existing --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can I just -- page 63 immediately before that is -- and I think the two pages after -- yeah, page 63 immediately before that is the beginning of that chapter, the two pages don't show the whole chapter but at least, perhaps, page 63 should be added to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, what are we going to do with these page numbers that I mentioned the day before yesterday, the witness spoke about that, I didn't have to show it to him because he was confirming that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Identify the page numbers you showed to the witness and consult with the Prosecution and come back to the Chamber if there is any problem. Mr. Sivac, that concludes your evidence. I would like to thank you on behalf of this Chamber and the Tribunal as a whole for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would also like to thank you for having the time and the patience to listen to me one more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will rise all together. We will have a break for half an hour and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dzafic. Do you hear me in the language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day. Yes, I can hear you in a language I can understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly swear that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dzafic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dzafic. Please state your full name.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I am Atif Dzafic, the son of Avdo, born in 1950 in Sanica and that is where I'm still living today.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Dzafic, as we discussed on the videolink the other day, part of your evidence in this case will be submitted in writing and we first need to deal with the formalities associated with that submission. You provided statements and information to representatives to the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY and you testified before the ICTY in two trials, the Brdjanin trial in 2002 and the Stanisic/Zupljanin trial on 4 and 5 February 2010; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You've recently had an opportunity to review, with the assistance of an interpreter, an amalgamated witness statement containing portions of your evidence from your statements and your Stanisic and Zupljanin testimony; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 90248 [sic] on the screen, please? Mr. Registrar, if the witness could be shown his amalgamated witness statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Dzafic, is that the document that you reviewed the other day?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is the document that I looked at a day or two ago here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: There are a small number of facts stated that need to be correct order clarified and if we could go quickly through these, in paragraph 1 on page 2 of the document, the fifth sentence, is it right that the dates 1985-1988 should read 1985-1990? That is, you studied at the Faculty of Political Science from 1985 to 1988 and submitted your dissertation in 1990? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You also studied at the Faculty of Political Science in Zagreb not in Zadar as it currently reads which is what you stated in your original statement in February 2001; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we did correct that. That is now correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In paragraph 2 also on that page, you stated that you did your JNA training at the reserve officers' school in Zadar, not in Zagreb as it currently reads and you corrected this in an addendum to your statement; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I assist? I think that the Serbian version is somebody else's statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karadzic, what's on the screen but the witness actually has a hard copy of the amalgamated witness statement in his hand.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Dzafic, if we could go to paragraph 6 on page 3?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, just to correct the transcript it should be 65 ter document 90284 [wrong translation on English channel].

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Court deputy, the interpretation was coming through in B/C/S not English. What was the number that you stated?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it should be 90284, amalgamated ICTY witness statement of Dzafic, Atif. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: My apologies, that was the number I read. Sorry. I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Dzafic, on paragraph 6 on page 3, it states that you were relieved of duty as commander of the Kljuc SJB on 21 May 1992. Can you just clarify that at that time you held the rank of commander of the police in the Kljuc public security station also known as the SJB? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes. Until 21, or rather, 22 May I was the commander of the police station in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You say commander of the police station in Kljuc. Were you --

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Since I did not sign the loyalty -- since I did not sign the loyalty document for the Serbian authorities, I was called on 22 or 21 May and then I was relieved of duty. My weapons, I handed over and I was told to leave the Kljuc police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Dzafic. That's all contained in the amalgamated witness statement. I simply want to know at this point in the position as commander of the police, you reported directly to the chief of the SJB, did you not?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: According to our laws, as the commander I was personally responsible to the chief, Kondic, for the tasks and responsibilities that I was entrusted with.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Dzafic, if I can now take you to paragraph 8 also on that page, the sentence reads: "The municipality of Kljuc had the following villages and hamlets within its borders:" And this should read: "The municipality of Kljuc had the following non-Serb villages and hamlets within its borders:"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes. These were non-Serb settlements in the territory of the Kljuc municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Finally, paragraph 24 on page 7, the sentence, "Kondic appointed Dusan Stojakovic as the deputy commander," should read, "Kondic appointed Dusan Stojakovic as the assistant commander"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Correct. Stojakovic, deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Ms. Sutherland, it's page 43, line 17, it's your question. You asked him from lines 16: [As read] "I simply want to know at this point in the position as commander of the police, you reported directly to the chief of the SJB, did you not."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So he was the commander of the Kljuc SJB and then he reported to the chief of that SJB? Was that your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes under the chief, there is another level at which the witness was at but I will ask him to, in fact, give that evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Dzafic, going back to paragraph 6 on page 3, it states there that you were relieved of duty as the commander of the Kljuc SJB.
