Your position at that time was as commander of the police, was it not, and in that position as commander of police, you reported directly to the chief of the SJB, who you referred to earlier as Mr. Kondic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And just a moment ago I read to you the correction that you wished to make to paragraph 24, where it had Kondic appointing Dusan Stojakovic as the deputy commander and it should have read he appointed him as the assistant commander, is that the correction you wanted to make?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you confirm, please, that with those corrections and clarifications the amalgamated statement accurately reflects your evidence?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If you were asked today about the matters contained in that statement, would you provide the same information to the Trial Chamber and that is even if you would probably not be able to formulate everything in the same words, the essence of your answers would be the same?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes. By all means, the answers, the gist, would be the same regardless of the time that has passed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender 65 ter 90284, the amalgamated witness statement of Mr. Dzafic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That is admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That shall be assigned Exhibit P3488.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: With Your Honour's leave I'll now read a short summary of the witness's evidence. Mr. Atif Dzafic was born and grew up in the Kljuc municipality. In 1997 the witness joined the police in Kljuc. Between 1978 and 1982, he was deputy commander of police and from 1982 to May 1992, he held the post of commander of the police. After the multi-party elections in 1990, he also held the position of acting chief of SJB until a Serb, Vinko Kondic, was appointed to the post of chief of police of the public security station. On 21 May 1992, the witness was relieved of his duty as commander of the police because he refused to sign a loyalty oath to the Serb authorities. The witness describes the SDS takeover of the municipality, the Serb Crisis Staff, the split of the police, the Serb Special Police unit, the deterioration in interethnic relations and the persecution of non-Serbs. He provides evidence of his own arrest and detention at the Nikola Mackic school which is schedule C, 15.2 and the Manjaca camp, schedule C, 1.2. The witness gives detailed descriptions of beatings, forced labour, inadequate nutrition and generally inhumane conditions at both camps. The witness provides information on other detention facilities including the SJB building in Kljuc which is schedule C, 15.1, the witness also provides evidence in relation to incidents at Biljani, schedule A, 7.3 and Velagici, schedule B, 10.1. The witness was released from Manjaca camp on 16 December 1992 when he was put on an escorted convoy to Karlovac in Croatia. In 1993, the witness met up with family members in Travnik and returned to Kljuc municipality in 1995 after its liberation. The witness attended exhumations conducted in the Kljuc municipality. That completes the summary of the witness's written evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Dzafic, I have a couple of questions or a few questions for you. If I could have 65 ter number 00262 on the screen, please, and this is, Mr. Registrar, this is document at tab 15 in your binder. Mr. Dzafic, this is a document that you saw the other day, dated 28 May 1992, to all SJBs in the region from Stojan Zupljanin at the CSB Banja Luka concerning the dismissal of those employees who did not --

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Security Services Centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, security services centre regarding the dismissal of those employees who did not sign the solemn declaration. Is that consistent with what you know happened in the SJB in Kljuc? You have testified already in your statement that it happened to you, but what about the other non-Serb police officers?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The speakers are overlapping.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Ms. Sutherland and Mr. Dzafic, because of the overlapping, we couldn't hear you. Could you start again your answer, kindly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gladly. I can see the dispatch by the Banja Luka Security Services Centre signed by Stojan Zupljanin, the chief and it was sent to all of the police stations in the Banja Luka region. It states that all the employees who did not sign the loyalty will have their employment terminated as of 15 April 1992, which is something that happened to me personally, as well as to other non-Serb staff at the public security station in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Dzafic. Your Honour, I tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document shall be assigned Exhibit number P3489. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter number 00849 and Mr. Registrar, this is at tab 13 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Dzafic, this is also a document you saw the other day. It's a War Presidency decision of 21 July 1992 signed by the president, Jovo Banjac, and it states at point 1, all managerial posts, positions where the inflow of information is possible at the protection of socially owned property and all places of importance for the functioning of economic entities may only be filled by staff of Serbian nationality, can be found. Item 2 also refers to all socially owned enterprises, shareholding companies, state institutions, public enterprises and the public security station. You've just advised us about what was happening in the SJB. What do you know about that happening in other public institutions?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: This was happening in all the other institutions, including state and public enterprises, and we mentioned my case at the police station, and this decision publicly talks about when the SDS won over 58.8 per cent of the power in the Kljuc municipality, indicating that something similar would happen, and so this is evidence that this was actually practically implemented, and as for disloyal Serbs, I can mention Dusan Petrovic, who was a commander of the TO staff before the elections but was not loyal to the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that is why later he was not appointed to this post any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Dzafic --

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: If necessary, I also remember --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: If required, I also recall other leading officials in the municipality who were non-Serbs and who were relieved of duty, and these are Enisa Ducanovic, Hamdija Ducanovic, the president of the Court, Dzemal Botonjic, the Prosecutor, Enisa Ducanovic and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did your wife also hold a managerial position?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I was actually -- when I mentioned my own case I meant myself and my wife who was in the Obnova company in a leadership position and on the same date she was sent to take her vacation on the same day that I was told to go, and she never returned to work again.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dzafic. I've finished with that document. If I could have 65 ter number 00873, and this is at tab -- Mr. Registrar, this is at tab 16 in the binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The previous document will be admitted as --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have something to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document could have been produced in 1995 when they reentered Prijedor. There is no protocol number and there is to signature. If we go back to the document, you will see that there is no protocol number on the original, and there is no signature. And the stamp was accessible to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us upload that document. 65 ter 849. So you are challenging the authenticity of this document, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, because at the top there is just the marking P501, and that could have been also issued by the presidential cabinet, but anyone could have signed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness has testified that what's contained, the contents that are contained in this document, are consistent with his knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, but we are talking about the authenticity.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I know that, Your Honour, but in relation to -- it's a matter for weight for Your Honours. It doesn't stop the document from being admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would also mention, Mr. President, and Mr. Robinson, I believe, will confirm this, the Defence has tendered innumerable documents with similar deficiencies that otherwise bear indications of authenticity. And I think a selective approach does not serve anyone's interest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But Mr. Karadzic is raising at the moment the possibility of making up of this document, if my understanding is correct. Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, we are not accepting the authenticity of this document. I do agree that there are other circumstances where documents which bear stamps and no signatures have been admitted but given that in this municipality the Bosniaks came to power and had access to these stamps, there is some legitimate basis to question the authenticity of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will mark it for identification until the time we are satisfied as to its provenance or authenticity. Yes, it will be marked for identification as Exhibit P3490. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, looking at the document, if we could go to the handwritten B/C/S pages which is at pages 16 to 24 of the document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the meantime, we will upload 873 on our part as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Dzafic, you reviewed this document. Do you recognise the handwriting?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could all unnecessary microphones be switched off, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do recognise this handwriting this is Todo Gajic's handwriting. He was inspector at the -- of the criminal police at the Kljuc police station, and he regularly visited Manjaca camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How long had you known Mr. Gajic for?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I had known Mr. Gajic from the first day when I started working at the police station, from September 1, 1970, up until the last day when I was relieved of duties and basically fired from the police. We --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: 1970, do you mean 1977?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: My apologies, September 1, 1977 until 21 May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And that document appears to be notes of a meeting in Manjaca camp; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so. And I see then further down my neighbours who were in Manjaca but who were ill on that particular day.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say something? The witness is not talking about the document that we see before us on our screen but, rather, about some documents that he has before him. Could we see those documents that he is referring to? And could my learned -- could Ms. Sutherland please show us the documents that the witness is actually looking at and share it with us?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Dzafic is looking at the document 00873. It's typewritten and it also has handwriting and there is a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So the first part, i.e. the e-court pages, 1 to 15, are typewritten parts and from 16 to 24 are the handwritten part [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... are the handwritten pages and that was the handwriting that the witness recognised as being that of Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: From the appearance it seems to be the case. As you can see from the monitor. Let's proceed, Ms. Sutherland. And then court deputy in the field office confirms that as well. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Dzafic, that is all the questions I have for you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender the associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before that we will admit this, 873 that will be Exhibit P3491. I have a few questions in relation to associated exhibits. First one relates to 65 ter number 874. In the transcript or in the statement, the witness confirmed his name, that number 685 is his, but the document does not have that number. It ends at number 67. Could we upload that exhibit, 65 ter number 874? So could you come back to us after checking it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I will do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And 65 ter number 920, which is a drawing of the witness, and 16080 do not have the English translation. I think at least the legend should be translated.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I will see to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Otherwise, are there any objections in relation to associated exhibits, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then all the others and these ones as well, those untranslated documents will be marked for identification in the meantime, and then I take it 874 will be supplemented later on by the Prosecution. With those caveats, we will admit them all and give a number in due course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Dzafic, you will now be asked by Mr. Karadzic, the accused, in his cross-examination. Please bear in mind that both you and Mr. Karadzic are speaking the same language. Please make sure that you put a pause between -- before you start answering the question. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Dzafic. Let us take a look, in view of the fact that you are speaking under oath here, let us take a look at what the truth and the whole truth actually is. In paragraph 4 of your statement, your amalgamated statement, you suggest that you were a police commander and that the SDA asked you to continue in that role, and you are suggesting now, or you suggest there actually, that you were asked to do this because you were an expert; right?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In other words, not because you were a member of that same party and not as a party official?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, let me clarify that a little bit. I had previously been a successful deputy commander, and then, following that, I served as the commander of the police in -- for two terms, although the second term was not completed. After that, the -- after the multi-party elections, SDA representatives asked to see me and then they asked me if I could continue and stay in that post, and I accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So as a non-party person; correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't sign any papers to the effect that I would be bound by the SDA. I simply agreed that I would remain in my post as commander of the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you a member of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: No. I don't want to go into the voting now, but I never officially signed any statement or any application in order to become a member of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now have 65 ter 22075, please? Let us see what you said in the Adamovic trial, and if we can have page 8 of that document, in other words document 22075, page 8. The ERN page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's not listed in your list of papers to be used with this witness. I'm not sure whether the court deputy in the field office has it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We notified that under the number 22074, but today they have actually switched the numbers and assigned it a new number, 22075.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there we have notified the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. It's 22074 says that it was the testimony. So court deputy in the field office should -- must have it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So now can we have page 8 of this document, yes, we have the right page. Now, please look at this, the Prosecutor Begovic asks you the following: {As read] "I understand that but you said that your party, if I understood it correctly, you talk about a coalition but what party did you belong to?" And you say, "Well, I was a member of the SDA," well, er -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it says there that I was a member, but you asked me a moment ago whether I signed any official documents for the SDA, and I can state here that I never did any such thing, but of course it says here that I was a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I didn't actually ask you about your signature. I only asked you whether you were a member of the SDA. And we have the answer now. Now, tell us, please, do you know when the SDA and when the SDS were established? Do you agree that the SDA was the first party to be established, both at the republic level and in your municipality?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 17, you talk about Alija Delimustafic. You say that after the election, he replaced Dusko Zgonjanin, who was a Serb; is that true?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: After the multi-party elections, the Ministry of the Interior, or rather, Alija Delimustafic was elected as the Minister of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But whom did he succeed?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, previously, the secretary of the secretariat or the minister was Dusko Zgonjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm afraid that too is incorrect, Mr. Dzafic. It was Muhamed Besic, a Muslim; right?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, I really can't recall, believe me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then in paragraph 18, you state that there were security station centres, security service centres in Banja Luka, Zenica, Doboj, Tuzla, Sarajevo, Mostar. Now, would you agree with me that only Banja Luka was a centre in an area that had an absolute Serb majority and Doboj where there was a relative Serb majority, whereas all the other centres were in areas that had a Serbian majority but not in the territorial sense but not a -- but they did not have centres there. Is Bihac, Gorazde, Zenica --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do not overlap, Mr. Karadzic. I don't know from where we missed. There was an answer to certain part of your question but we missed it. Please continue. But on your part, please put a pause.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. My apologies to participants and to Witness Dzafic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said, Witness, that you never gave any thought to that, but you do agree that only Banja Luka had the Serb majority; correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me then repeat for the transcript: Bihac, Gorazde, Zenica, Tuzla, Sarajevo, Mostar and Livno had centres but they did not have a Serb majority; correct? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, off the top of my head I really can't say. I never really looked at the ethnic structure within these various security services centres. I knew about the Banja Luka area. I knew that there was a predominantly Serb population there, but as for the other centres I really can't say either way, simply I never looked into that. I was not interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 22, you describe that Stojan Zupljanin was appointed or elected after some other candidates actually withdrew their candidatures; correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: According to some information that I had, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, do you know that we had to fight a big battle there and that the SDS preferred candidate was a completely different person but he did not work in the police and Zupljanin who was not a member of the SDS was appointed at the proposal of the deputy minister, Zepinic?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But then would you agree that paragraph 22 is incorrect?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, there were two other candidates. They withdrew from running for Banja Luka CSB chief, and they told me that they had been offered this post but that they refused to accept it, but how correct that is, I never checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 16, you say that Dusko Petrovic succeeded Jovo Kevac in the Territorial Defence and that after Dusko Petrovic, Bosko Lukic was elected. Was Bosko Lukic a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, you actually put several questions, Mr. Karadzic, all at once. I don't really know whether Mr. Lukic was a member of the SDS or not. I know that he was a retiree and that he was reactivated after a while, that he was brought back to perform that duty. As for the second question or rather the first, I know that both Dusan Petrovic held this duty of TO Staff Commander, as well as Kevac, and I know very well that after the multi-party election, Dusan Petrovic was not elected to that post.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you are now stressing the party membership and you pointed out that Bosko Lukic was nominated by the SDS. So I'm asking you whether Bosko Lukic was appointed to the Territorial Defence post because he was a member of the SDS or because people trusted his abilities, his competence, and in that context, do you know whether he was a member of the SDS or not?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, I just said a moment ago that I don't know specifically about Lukic but according to everything we could see and what was happening with that post I know that Lukic could not have been appointed to that post without having been a member of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you stand by that? You claim that with certainty?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who was the president of the municipality of Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: At what time, what time period are you talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, after the multi-party election?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: It was Mr. Jovo Banjac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And who was the president of the municipality before the multi-party elections?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I can't remember. I would need some time to reflect on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could it have been Jovo Banjac still?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I think so. I think it was Jovo, but I'm not absolutely certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In other words, Jovo Banjac was not president of the municipality because he was a member of the SDS but because he had some experience in that job - correct? - so that in his case that too was the case.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when Vinko Kondic was appointed as the chief of the public security station, that was the post that was apportioned to the SDS, he had some difficulties and there were some issues raised, so that his appointment was delayed; correct? You speak about this in paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that he had been convicted to a prison term of six months, that he appealed and that the appeal was supported and then only after that he was appointed to that post?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, let me clarify that a bit, Mr. Karadzic. Vinko Kondic was supposed to be appointed together with me. It was delayed by a few months because there was -- there were criminal proceedings underway against Vinko for some irregularities in the company where he worked, of which he was -- with which he was charged. However, the Court decision was not final and after the appeals proceedings where he was acquitted, he was appointed. He was relieved of these accusations and he was appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And he was appointed as the chief of the public security station?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes. And he had --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Could you repeat your answer, after you had said yes, Mr. Dzafic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you mean my answer to the last question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Dzafic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, the last, the appointment --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I just intervene? My question was not recorded in the transcript. I said that before he was appointed, you -- you were acting chief of police station and police commander, and you answered affirmatively, you said yes.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, for a while I held both those posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, when he was nominated, you were left with just one of those functions, the commander of the station; correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, if I put it to you, Mr. Dzafic, that this whole matter with the court proceedings were recognised by the Serb side as the well-known framing, system of framing people, in order to interfere with their appointment, what would you answer?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I have nothing to say to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, thank you. You told me that the president of the court advised you of these things; correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: The president of the court and other people who were saying that Vinko's appointment was delayed precisely for these reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The president of the court was Dzemo Botonjic, whom you mentioned a little earlier, when you said that he was fired; correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your interview of 1998, document 65 ter 22073, this portion can be found on page 3. And the same is true of the English translation, page 3. And in document 22074, also on page 3, you said -- you state as follows. So can we have document 22074 or 22075, whatever you call it now? Can we pull up that document, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it that the transcript in Adamovic, we do not have the English translation; correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, we do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then the e-court has a mistake. It refers to another transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first document is 22073 on page 3. You say, "As I heard from the president of the court, Dzemo Botonjic ...," whereas in this document, 22074, on page 3, you say as follows: [As read] "Well, let me be succinct. I never said in any statement that I had heard this directly from Dzemo. Rather, I heard it from other people that Mr. Botonjic was complaining that there were pressures relating to this case and that this should be take be care of as soon as possible." So did you hear this from the judge, the president of the court, or from someone else? Which of these two versions is correct.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, I remember clearly that the president of the court was Mr. Dzemo Botonjic, that the Prosecutor was Dragan Kojic, and the judge was Enisa Botonjic. In conversations with them, I know that Dzemo, the president, told me on one occasion, and this was unofficial, that they were waiting for the appointment of Mr. Kondic's precisely for this reason, that that's why it was being delayed. I won't repeat it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: He said that to you; right?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were talking in an informal conversation, and that's when he told me that. And there were stories going around in the police, among the leadership, people were saying that we were going to get a new chief, Vinko Kondic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But the Adamovic trial on page 3 you said it was not him who told you that, it was other people?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, my memory is not getting better with time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, let me see the ERN number of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: While we are waiting, sorry to interrupt but page 62, line 2, Mr. Karadzic said, "In your interview of 1998 ...,." I think he meant 2008, did he not?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I apologise. 22073 is the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just briefly, Mr. Dzafic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is not 22075, Mr. Karadzic? You referred to the transcript in Adamovic case.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, maybe I was not quite clear. One document is 22073, that's a statement from 2008. Whereas his testimony is 22074, testimony in the Adamovic trial, and these two testimonies are different. And I would like to find out what is what, but, okay, we got an answer now. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzafic, you mentioned Dzemo Botonjic as president of the court. You mentioned another Botonjic as a judge. Who is the other one?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: No. As far as I remember, there was only one Botonjic working at the court. There was also a lady, Enisa Ducanovic, a judge at the time and later she became a Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned a lady by the surname of Botonjic working at the court. Did such a person exist?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Not that I remember, Mr. Karadzic. There was no lady by the name of Botonjic working at the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 24, you made a correction today saying that Dusan Stojakovic was not your deputy but your assistant. What happened with Dusan Stojakovic, your assistant? What became of him?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: It is true that he was assistant commander, appointed by the chief, Vinko Kondic. Now, this question what became of Stojakovic, I can only answer by explaining this: After my removal from the police on 22 May 1992, with my wife who was also removed from her work, and with two children who were attending primary school, and that particular school year was ended prematurely, one or two months earlier than normal, I went to my native village of Sanica, and I stayed there until the day of my arrest, 1 June. As to all the things that happened on 27 May, when my former colleague Dusan Stojakovic, was killed in the neighbourhood of Krasulje, I don't know. There were all kinds of stories and rumours circulating, and the investigation was conducted by the people who were then employed at the police station of Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But one indisputable fact remains that he was killed in a Muslim neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: He was killed on the road, Pudin Han to Sanski Most, just outside the settlement of Krasulje, somewhere there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And that's one of those settlements that you described as non-Serb?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that your party, just after the elections and after your appointment, put pressure on you to balance out the ethnic composition of the police force?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: There were talks between parties, and I was sent a letter saying that I should balance the ethnic composition of the senior staff in the police, because Kljuc municipality had an area of 800.000 square metres, and a population that is 7.000. There were 42 per cent Muslims and much less Serbs, but that was not reflected among the senior staff in the police, although it all depends on what you define as senior post. Out of nine senior posts, only two were occupied by Muslims, and that's why this letter, this circular, came that the ethnic composition among the senior staff should be balanced, but the chief, Vinko Kondic, did not comply. On the contrary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So even after -- even before the elections, you were both acting chief and commander of the station, and during your tenure, the ethnic composition of the senior staff was not balanced?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, for a short period, even before the multi-party elections, I was acting chief, but that was not for long. That was just two or three months, because the chief was suspended at the time and I was acting chief very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Which chief was suspended?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: That was president of the court, Rajko Dakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you actually inherited this imbalance from the Socialist period, from the previous regime, and your political party asked you to make adjustments?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: They asked Vinko to do that because in my particular position I could not change anything in the personnel composition of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that in the Adamovic case, 65 ter 22074, page 7, the ERN number is 0623-0511 [as interpreted]. You said the party to which I belonged wanted to balance the ethnic composition also among the senior staff and all the other employees of the station.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Let me just find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking, yes, although putting it this way, perhaps it should have been phrased differently but, basically, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Considering that those were professionals who were employed, you were supposed to dismiss a number of people and hire another number of people?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: You couldn't say that really because, at the police station the commander of the section or the squad, the police, was a Muslim and we were supposed to hire in his place somebody of the same ethnicity but we instead hired a commander of a different ethnic group, Milan Tomic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You speak about that in paragraph 25 of your amalgamated statement, which reflects part of your testimony in that case, and you say that this Sejdo Adzimovic was replaced by a Serb by the name of Tomic. Isn't it rather the case that Tomic did not replace him, the other man was retired?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Adzimovic was retired, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So he was not replaced in order to appoint Tomic?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, if you retire, you're not really replaced, so, yes, you're right. I don't know why this word is suddenly so important but I see it's important. Anyway, it's not up to me. It's up to the person who took the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But what was the composition of the police station in that local commune?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: You mean in the entire municipality of Kljuc or in the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The police station.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, as for the police station, at the police station, sometimes had a staff of only six to eight. Half would be one group, half of the other, but I can't really answer this precisely because personnel changes were frequent. Some people moved to the police station in Kljuc. And you know the ethnic composition of the local commune of Sanica, at least I think you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's majority Muslim, but is it true that the majority of the police personnel was also Muslim?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Sometimes it was 50/50. Sometimes there was one Bosniak more than the number of Serbs. As far as I remember, it was half/half.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 26, you talk about the changes in the police station in Kljuc, and you say somewhere in line 4 that Kondic had the door to his office closed all the time and you go on to say that he received frequent visits by Veljko Kondic and Jovo Banjac and you enumerate all the Serbs in that paragraph 26, and then you say that he never told you what was discussed at those meetings. You say also that you had -- you saw President Banjac visit Veljko Kondic a number of times. Why is that unusual, Mr. Dzafic? Why is it unusual for the president of the municipality to visit the chief of the police?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: It wouldn't have been unusual if it had happened in our working hours, and if I, as police station commander, had also been invited.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But did you all socialise among yourselves over there? Could there have been private encounters?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, I knew Mr. Veljko and Mr. Jovo both privately and from work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What I'm trying to say is that paragraph 26 makes certain implications. For one, that Serbs were seeing each other, that the chief did not inform you of his discussions with these people, and there is another implication, that you were keeping an eye on the Serbs and perhaps they were keeping an eye on you?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I can say that I wasn't keep an eye on anyone. I wasn't keeping tabs but from all my earlier experience I was able to make a judgement when the chief of the station was justified in talking to the president of the municipality without my knowledge. However, there were certain matters that I should have been informed of, instead of having my deputy attend those meetings and do this work that actually belonged to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: From all of this, do you agree that with the appointment of Vinko Kondic, you lost a more important position of the chief, and remained just commander, and that you were in a rivalry with Kondic?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Again, there are several questions in one. Let me take them one by one. I was actually relieved when Kondic took over the position of chief, because I didn't have to do two jobs at once any more. Second, I never felt there was any rivalry between me as commander and Mr. Kondic. All I wanted was good co-operation and good work, professional work, in a lawful manner, as I had been taught and trained. Because I was commended and awarded with the highest awards that could be obtained at the Ministry of the Interior for my prior work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 29, which is part of your testimony, you say that there had been cases of contradictory orders, from Banja Luka and from Sarajevo, mutually contradictory orders. Did that really happen?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How do you explain that? How did orders come to be contradictory?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I'll try to explain it in very simple terms. I remember well one dispatch --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I thought it was 29. I can check but it could also be 30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed, Mr. Dzafic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try to give you an example that I remember very clearly, to explain those contradictory orders, dispatches from Banja Luka and dispatches from Sarajevo. Early in April, I don't know exactly when but I was still working, and it was on a night shift, a dispatch came from the Security Services Centre Banja Luka, addressed directly to the chief, asking us to send to Bosanska Krupa a team of I don't know exactly how many policemen to assist them, but the policemen should be exclusively Serbs because they had problems of I don't know what nature, it doesn't matter now, and I just happened to see this dispatch. The operator showed it to me. And that operator also had certain problems with the chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, later -- I don't know if you want to hear about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I want to know if the public security station in Kljuc was part of the Security Services Centre in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Naturally it was but those dispatches and those orders, I called Sarajevo, by the way, and they were astonished by that dispatch.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, that was helpful. You say that you fell under the jurisdiction of the security services centre in Banja Luka, and yet you communicated directly with Sarajevo, circumventing your own CSB and your own chief.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Those were not communications of God knows what importance, but I was just talking to them to see what I'm supposed to do. Why I, as a commander, was left out of the loop? Why wasn't I supposed to know about this dispatch.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you were bypassing the chief, Vinko Kondic, and you also circumvented your CSB in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, the main command was in Sarajevo, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Command has its own chain, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes. There is a chain of command, but if a lower-level decision is not lawful, is not regular, then I think one must seek a second opinion from the higher command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So we do agree there is a chain of command. Is there also a chain of reporting?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do we agree that this chain should not be broken? You always go to your immediate superior?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, you had these contacts with Sarajevo. To whom did you talk in Sarajevo, circumventing Kondic and Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Any contacts I had were with the inspector who was in charge of inspection and auditing of the police station in Kljuc, who came once a year for an annual inspection. I don't remember the name of that inspector but on one occasion he -- or, rather, Mr. Avdo Hebib contacted me directly when the refugees from Knin were passing through Kljuc and the dispatch was sent to tell us that we should let this convoy pass through Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We will come to that. But you have stated that you communicated directly with Mr. Avdo Hebib, who was assistant minister for the police.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I just told you, yes, not every day but as required.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Weren't you breaking the chain of command and the chain of reporting by doing so?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: It all depends on the circumstances I was in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember receiving, on 29 April -- in fact, did you also receive on 12 April an order from Hasan Efendic to start an attack against the JNA and the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: No. I don't recall any such document, nor do I know Hasan Efendic to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we briefly show to the witness D400? Towards the end of April, did you receive from your minister a directive, an order, to start a war against the JNA? Could you take a look, to all security services centres, to all public security stations, and to the SUP of Sarajevo. Are you familiar with this document? It's an order dated 29 April 1992, the presidency had accepted this decision of their own Territorial Defence, and it was sent to you through the ministry?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: This is the first time I see it, Mr. Karadzic. I've never seen this before and I don't know what's written in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see that it says, on the 27th of April, it was adopted. Do you know what was going on in the valley of the Sana river on 24 April and 27 April? Do you know what was going on in Prijedor, in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it the break now or has the schedule changed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you continue for three minutes more?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll be happy to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 32, you speak about check-points and you say they were set up in the second half or in the autumn of 1991; right?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: If that's what my statement says, then it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that you stated there were these check-points at the access -- at the entry point to Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were check-points.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that they were manned by joint, mixed police patrols and there were also military policemen and servicemen on these teams?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: In the beginning, there were only professional policemen and reserve policemen, and then the military police and the army joined in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did this coincide with the outbreak of the war in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The routes of arms smuggling, desertion from the army, the travel of sabotage groups, do they lead through Kljuc as well as other municipalities in Krajina?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there any arms smuggling? Were there deserters and renegades and those elements out of control at that time?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: There were many cases of soldiers returning from the war in Croatia, reservists who were natives of Kljuc, who did not return their weapons, who kept them, and then disturbed law and order and that was a threat to the safety of the citizens and the police had to intervene.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That was the police of Kljuc and they were later joined by the military police and army troops to deal with the problem?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was one problem but there were also other problems, and those problems were not dealt with properly at the beginning. The police should have taken weapons away from such people who were shooting around and disturbing peace. Active police would indeed seize those weapons from such people. But after two or three days, Mr. Vinko would return the weapons to such former soldiers or fighters or deserters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Or he would return it to the army, the military police; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, to the military police. After a day or two the same weapons would then find -- be found with those members, the same ones from whom it was confiscated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Break, is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Dzafic, we will have a break for an hour and resume at 1.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.33 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzafic, you're an expert on All People's Defence. That is indeed your profession; correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I graduated from the faculty of political sciences, the department for national defence and protection. Now, whether I'm an expert in that, well, I leave that to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In respect of these measures, the surveillance and control, you are competent to actually state whether, in view of the imminent threat of war, these check-points were in fact justifiable, in order to make sure that controls and checks were made to stop illegal trafficking of weapons and so on?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, I was never informed of the existence of the check-points. I learned about the check-points and of the existence of an order to that effect, to establish check-points, in other words, and I only learned of that here as a witness. Now, the law was complied with consistently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, would you agree with me that the civilian police was not authorised to search and stop military personnel; correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: The civilian police did have the right to intervene in matters involving military personnel but then they would have to inform the military police immediately of such incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the civilian police can intervene only in the course of the commission of a criminal act? As soon as that criminal act is over, they would have to transfer the case to the military police; correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure I understood your question. Would you please repeat it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If the civilian police were to actually intercept a military person in the act of committing a criminal offence, they would be authorised to intervene, but then, outside of that, they would have to refer the case to the military police?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. In the cases of, let's say, traffic accidents and similar matters, they would have that authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, would we agree that the police and the military, especially in the imminent threat of war, are part and parcel of an overall system of defence of any given country?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, the police and the military were part of the armed forces of our former common country.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: They were part of one unique system; correct? One unified system?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that people wanted, and called for, mixed check-points and for mixed police patrols where the patrols would consist of members of all three ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. And we tried to implement that, and we actually were successful for a while, and that was very effective as a tool, whenever we had these mixed patrols consisting of police officers from each one of these ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then at one point in time they ceased to be mixed patrols; correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, after certain incidents that occurred, problems arose, and then for a while this system was no longer effective and it ceased altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And this happened when police officers of Muslim ethnicity refused to declare their loyalty and implement the laws of Republika Srpska; correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, you've put several questions to me. I can say this: On two occasions, at two meetings, we were forced to sign a loyalty oath to the Serb authorities, but we refused to do that. After our second refusal, we were all dismissed and sent home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, let's clarify things a bit. When you started working for the police, did you have to take an oath, an oath of office?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, of course, naturally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then, when Republika Srpska was established, you were offered to do that. Were you forced to sign an oath of loyalty, or were you offered to sign it and continue with your work?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, it was offered to us to sign the loyalty oath, but in the environment that existed at the time, and all the discussions going on and so on, our impression was that it was, in fact, being imposed on us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, but let's see this. Did the Serbs have to sign an oath of loyalty?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, of course, the Serbs, too, signed oaths of loyalty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And that was one of the conditions for their being able to be employed in the police force; correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were then placed on furlough of a couple of weeks and then you were asked again whether you were willing to sign this oath of loyalty and continue or resume your office?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, the first meeting was held on the 7th of May, and the second meeting was held around the 21st or the 22nd of May. And after this second meeting, we were sent home. We were fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will revisit this issue. But now let's take a look at paragraph 35 of your statement. You state there that the declaration of independence of Slovenia and Croatia had a negative effect on the quota system where there were differences between --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: They had a negative effect on Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the consequence was that it would not join the rump Yugoslavia and would go against the Serb wishes to remain within Yugoslavia. Now, can we just clarify the terminology here: Why would Bosnia have to join Yugoslavia when it was already a member of Yugoslavia? That is a contradiction, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't have an answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But, legally, this is relevant. Now, you say that the position of the Bosnian Presidency was not to join the rump Yugoslavia. However, legally speaking, Bosnia was already part of Yugoslavia, and it wasn't necessary for it to join, and that was not a request or a call for Bosnia to join rump Yugoslavia but, rather, to leave it; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, it's a question of terminology.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, in that case, I believe we should leave in this paragraph the word "to remain." So the position of the Bosnian Presidency was that they refused to remain in the rump Yugoslavia rather than not to join the rump Yugoslavia; correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In other words, the Bosnian Presidency was calling for the -- an amendment to the constitution or, rather, the change in the constitutional position of Bosnia within Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, for me, that's high-level politics. Don't ask me about that. You're asking about the Presidency's decision. Don't. I don't know anything about that, believe me. At the time when I was employed, I never thought about high-level politics, even at the time when I was in this position and let alone now. So, please, would you refrain from these questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Mr. Dzafic. I would gladly do so; however, your paragraph 35 actually introduces that topic. So I would like to explore whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does it make a very big difference whether or not the witness used the words "join" or "remain"? I would like you to come to the real issues. Your time is limited.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then, would you please address this with the Prosecutor because they should not include irrelevant issues in an exhibit of theirs, because if it's irrelevant or insignificant, why did it find its place in paragraph 35?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 36, Witness, you talk about rumours and stories going around about Serbs being armed and that you yourself did not see that for yourself but you heard of it from some police officers; correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you start an investigation into that issue?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: No. Because in those circumstances it was impossible to launch an investigation into such a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was it impossible to launch an investigation perhaps because the JNA was, in fact, establishing its reserve units on the ground?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't think -- or, rather, I think it was impossible to launch an investigation because the outcome would have been negative anyway because no one, no civilians in the area where this was going on, was willing to talk about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you say that there were helicopters involved, that these young men went to Croatia in an organised manner to take part in combat there. Isn't that something that is reminiscent of reserve units in the JNA and which are on stand-by and once they're called up they would be deployed? Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, let's put it that way, yeah. Maybe you could say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in the same paragraph, you say that occasionally police officers of Serb nationality went to Knin for training, but did you know that the SDA had long before that sent Muslims for training to the Croatian MUP and ZNG long before that?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, this is a two-pronged question. As for the first part, it is correct that people were sent from Kljuc without my having any knowledge of it, as the police commander. People were sent for police training to Knin, and these were -- many of these people had police records, were criminals. I know of that for sure. Now, as for the other part of the question, whether the police was sent for training to Croatia, police officers of Muslim ethnicity, I put it to you that there were no such cases in Kljuc, nor do I know of any such cases, nor -- but there were some cases in other municipalities perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you trying to say that police cadets are criminals?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: No. Mr. Karadzic, in order for a person to be admitted as a police cadet, they would have to be checked. There would have to be a background check done. And these ten or so police officers who had been sent to Knin for training, they were not cadets. They were grown men. They were sent from various companies and work organisations to be trained in Knin.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did the Muslims apply for this and then were denied?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, or, in any case, I didn't know anything of any lists or their being sent for training. I only learnt about it when they started coming home for weekends, over the weekend, to visit their families. I did not send any police officers of Muslim ethnicity to any courses, so I don't have information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in paragraph 36 you talk about police cadets and that they applied voluntarily and that Muslims did not apply or report. Now, do you know whether there was a case that a Muslim person applied to be sent to Knin and was refused?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I don't have any information to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, is it correct that you sent mostly Muslims to Vrace in Sarajevo for training?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: There was a police academy at Vrace, and a select group of cadets from Kljuc municipality was sent to that academy. Now, whether they were predominantly Muslim or of other ethnicity, I don't know. Now, had they been Muslims predominantly, the ethnic break-up -- the ethnic composition would not be as it was on the 21st of April when no Serbs were fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, do you know what the ethnic composition of the reserve police force was?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, you discussed the arming of Serbs, but did you know anything about the arming of Muslims at the time?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, the arming of either group was illegal. It was difficult to obtain any information about either group, and in any case such information would not reach me, but there was -- weapons were distributed to non-Bosniak villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did you know - and I believe that you talked about this - did you know that there was the establishment of two municipalities of Kljuc were -- was underway?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about the division of the territory of the municipality of Kljuc. There were stories and gossip going around, but there was no division for as long as I was in Kljuc, at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was the municipality of Bosnian Kljuc ever declared as such, as well as the Territorial Defence of Bosnian Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I learned later that Omer Filipovic was appointed commander of the Territorial Defence of Kljuc. I did not have an occasion to see anything. Later on, in the camp, after I was arrested, I learned all that. I don't know what territory was Serb and what territory was Muslim. I didn't know it then. I did not have an occasion to see that document. I was not even aware of any such document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, is that the same Omer Filipovic who was the vice-president of the joint assembly?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the same person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were number one man in the police from the Muslim ethnic group. Were you duty-bound to be a member of the staff of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Nobody ever asked me to join. Nobody ever told me anything about that staff, the staff of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we now look at D1730. That's a document that has already been admitted. I would like to jog your memory and I would like you to tell me whether you know the people referred to in the document. D1730. Do you see the document? It's an Official Note.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I'm reading the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know these people, Omer Filipovic, Amir Avdic, Nevzat Djeric, and so on and so forth, the commanders?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I am looking at the document now. I knew Mr. Filipovic. I knew Amir Avdic less. I didn't know Djeric at all. As for Salih Salihovic, I didn't know him. I knew another Salihovic, not this one. I didn't know of the existence of the staff of the so-called Bosanski Kljuc or Bosnian Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that before the new year the Muslim municipality of Bosanski Kljuc was declared?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at 65 ter 7842 -- or, rather, 17842. 17842.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know Esad Bender?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: The first time I heard of Esad Bender, and I saw him, was at Manjaca when he was killed. That was at the Manjaca camp in number 1 barn.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at this document. He says in here that he was not Omer and Mohamed Filipovic's body guard, that it was his brother. And in the third paragraph he speaks about the purchase of weapons. And he says that it was done upon the recommendation of Crisis Staffs. Do you remember that every Muslim local commune had its own Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, Mr. Karadzic, where I was moving around, where I stayed, as far as I know, there were no Crisis Staffs. There may have been some groups that looked after the safety of non-Serbian settlements and people. That's possible. And as for the staffs and their functioning, I didn't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the second paragraph, could you look at what it says. There is reference to the purchase of weapons even as far as Switzerland. It says here that Asim Egrlic issued certificates or documents on behalf of the party and then the weapons would be purchased. Is that the same Asim Egrlic who was the president of the joint Executive Board of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, look, again, this is a multi-pronged question. I don't know what Asim Egrlic did, but I know that after the election he did discharge those duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the end do you see where it says that Omer was told that they had captured seven soldiers and that four of them were killed? That's the last sentence on this page.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Look, I've never seen this document before. It would be wrong for me to give you my views of it or to discuss it. There is no signature, there is no stamp. This was compiled by an authorised official. This is an operative document which may be accurate or not, so it would be wrong for me to provide any comments upon this document. I wouldn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we go to the following page. He mentions the same names that are mentioned in your statement when you spoke about the arrest and the political life in your municipality. And even your name is mentioned here in the third paragraph, perhaps the 15th line from the bottom of the page. In the second paragraph, it says that Esad thinks and according to Mohamed and Omer told him that the agreement between the Muslims and the Serbs would have been signed but that Alija and rightists did not want that? Did you know that the MBO cooperated with us in order to sign the historical agreements between the Serbs and the Muslims? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, that was in July and August, and the whole of the state of Bosnia reverberated with the talks about that agreement. How come you didn't hear anything about that in the media?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go on. Let's see how he describes the Crisis Staff that existed in the premises -- or, rather, it is known that once he dropped by the SDA and found Omer Filipovic, Muhamed, Atif Dzafic, the former commander, Asim Egrlic, Hamdija Ducanovic, Omer's wife Merima, Fikret Balagic, and so on and so forth, many members of the Crisis Staff among them. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that. I can see my name. But this is not correct. At that time I did not attend any such meeting. I'm telling you now this is the signature of an authorised official, an authorised official whose signature is illegible. This is just the result of some checks from the field which can be accurate or not. We can discuss that. But as for me attending any such meeting, I can tell you that I didn't. You said that it was a Crisis Staff, but I really don't know. I've never seen this before, and I'm testifying truthfully, under oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not --

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Let me just tell you this, and I hope you will agree with me: If this were correct and accurate, if this were accurate and if my name was correctly put here, I would not have returned alive from Manjaca, Mr. Karadzic, and we would not have an occasion to talk today. And I claim this with full responsibility. If anything could have been pinned to my name, if there had been a document pinning some blame on me, I would not have returned alive from Manjaca. I am the only police commander who survived Manjaca and returned from Manjaca alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm glad to hear that. Thank you. However, the Serbs knew that about you on the 21st of June while you were at Manjaca. And let's go on reading. It says at that meeting there were discussions and a decision was reached that the headquarters of the Muslim --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We set a time -- amount of time for your cross-examination. That's why I let you continue. But having heard from the witness that he doesn't know anything about this, what's the point of continuing to put questions in relation to document? It's totally a waste of time, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, the last sentence states that he was earmarked as the commander of the Muslim police station. How come he didn't know anything about that? I will accept it if he says he didn't. But this is very important for his credibility and for painting the overall picture of the situation in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that you were earmarked as the commander of the Muslim police station? That's the last sentence in this document.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I didn't know. Let's be very clear, very specific: I didn't know that I was earmarked for any such position. If I had known this and, I repeat, if anybody else had known that, I would not have left Manjaca alive. There's no chance in hell that I would have left Manjaca alive if anybody had had a discussion to that effect with me and if I had accepted to be the police chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm denying this, Witness. The Serbs knew it on the 21st, and you still returned alive. This statement was taken on the 21st of June, 1992. And you were within their reach but they did not touch you. They didn't do anything to you; right?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: That's again the same question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's look at 1D4281. Did you believe the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina, not the Republika Srpska, but Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say "believe"? I worked for them. I joined the Ministry of the Interior in Sarajevo, and I thought, I believed, that if anything happened, that they would be the ones who would discharge me of my duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Look at the document issued by the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina, State Security Service in Tuzla. They received information from Omer Veladzic, who said that he had received 400 rifles from the Croatian government, in June 1991, in Bosanska Dubica, which had a 70 per cent Serbian majority. Junuz Bosic received 400 rifles from Croatia, right, isn't that what it says here? And then it says something about Kljuc further a bit down. He says that the rifles were sold to Muslims in Kljuc at 800 German marks apiece and that this man made 320.000 German marks, and this can be confirmed by Smajil Draganovic from Kljuc and Rasim Kulenovic from Bosanska Dubica. Did you know that in your municipality Muslims were purchasing rifles at 800 German marks each?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: When it comes to selling weapons and arming of Muslims in Kljuc, I didn't have any information to that effect. And this document was issued in September 1993. At that time, around 500 Muslims remained in the territory of Kljuc, no more than that, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
