utterances.text: I don't know how many permutations we've been through with this, but the question Dr. Karadzic posed at the end of the course is permissible, but the Court has admonished him repeatedly about the use of such documents and we spent time hearing through his recitation of the document which the Court has encouraged him -- of a document of the type the Court has encouraged him not to use. It's quite a continually pointless exercise.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I disagree. I'm not tendering this. But the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Reading out documents which will not be admitted is of no point, Mr. Karadzic, at all.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to confront the witness with the fact that right before his nose, where he was the commander of the police, weapons were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you remember the conversation between the Chamber -- well, not conversation, but debate between Chamber and Mr. Robinson. You should put your question first. And if witness denies, you can put some certain documents to a certain extent. Reading out documents which are not admitted without doubt is waste of time. You put your case -- question, or put your case to the witness. Even if your reading is to be reflected in the transcript, that means nothing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. I believe that I did that. I asked the witness about the arming of Muslims and he said that he didn't know anything about that. I believe that in his position he should have known about that. And now we have a Muslim source confirming that to have been the fact. But I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Just one sentence, if I may. Mr. Karadzic, you see, this was sent from the State Security Service in Tuzla on the 17th of September, 1993. At that time, I really don't know where I was. That was after Manjaca and after everything else. I was released from Manjaca and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, Mr. Dzafic, this person speaks about the events that had taken place in 1991. Croatia sent weapons to Dubica and then the weapons were sold in Kljuc. This is what the document is about.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Let me just say this: I wasn't privy to that information. As to whether such things were happening, whether the allegations are correct, this should be checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, as a person who's familiar with the Law on All People's Defence, is desertion a crime in our midst as everywhere else in the world?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sabotaging mobilisation, is that a crime?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, now you are -- under what conditions? What? In principle, desertion is a crime. In principle. But under what conditions, for what reasons? I wouldn't go into that. This is rather a political matter, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And sabotaging a mobilisation drive, is that a crime?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was, it is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us see what you say in paragraph 38. You mention Mr. Izetbegovic, who anecdotally recommended that Muslims should not respond to mobilisation calls. He himself said that he would not encourage his own son to respond. The entire paragraph deals with the fact that the Muslim population did not respond to mobilisation calls. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Listen, I was not involved in any mobilisations, and you have just paraphrased something that I heard on TV, in the media. I heard that as something that Mr. Izetbegovic had stated, and I can't comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, you provided this statement, and you say that only a few -- or, rather, very few Muslims responded. That's in your paragraph 38. And it becomes clear from that paragraph that Muslims did not respond to call-ups and that they were inspired to do so by Mr. Izetbegovic; right?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: When I was giving that statement, I said clearly that a certain number of people enlisted. When they got to their units and received assignments, that's when they deserted. And then the news spread across Kljuc municipalities and other people were discouraged from responding to mobilisation call-ups.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then in paragraph 40 you called those soldiers Serb soldiers. Is it the case that in end 1991 those were Serb soldiers, or were they, rather, soldiers of the JNA and they were Serb only because Croats and Muslims failed to respond to call-ups?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I don't have that statement before me. I cannot comment. There are many issues at stake and many questions in one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 40.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Repeat your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say, towards the end of 1991, when Serb soldiers were returning from the war in Croatia and so on and so forth. I want to know what you understand by the term "Serb soldiers."

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: What is implied here under that term are reservists who had responded to the mobilisation call-up, who enlisted to go to war in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But the army is not the Serbian army, it's the JNA, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: They wore the old insignia of the former JNA army at that time, in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then you said in the same paragraph that Radio Kljuc broadcast in a biassed manner, in favour of Serbs and preserving Yugoslavia and against secession; right?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I know Radio Kljuc was active. Now, as to your specific question, all I have is the English version. I can't understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you have signed this statement, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Of course I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In this statement you also say that Serbs dug up their mortal remains of dead Serbs outside churches and reburied them. I have to make this clear to the Trial Chamber. Are Serbs crazy to dig up bones from one grave and rebury them in another or was it the case that Serbs were recovering for the first time the mortal remains of dead Serbs from various pits and mass graves and buried them in proper graves? Which is the case?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I did not look into that problem in any detail, but generally speaking there were cases when those bones were dug up and Serbdom was celebrated, and that increased tensions in Kljuc. That only deteriorated the general situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it the case that mortal remains were recovered from pits and mass graves where they were initially put by the Ustasha and buried in proper graves, or was it the case that Serbs were taking bones out of one grave and buried them in another?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know much about it. But following simple logic, I suppose they were recovered to be properly buried.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the editorial programming board of Radio Kljuc, were there any Muslims employed, including Omer Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Omer Filipovic was a teacher of history and the history of language at the secondary school. I don't know if he was involved in Radio Kljuc. Maybe he was providing some news items for a while, but I don't think he was employed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, the programming board does not consist necessarily of full-time staff. Those could be prominent citizens from the town.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I don't think -- I don't remember he was in the programming board.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But he often spoke on Radio Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was there often or not, but he was occasionally a guest in various programmes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 42, you speak of the murder of Senad Dervisevic, a Muslim in his 20s, who was killed by gunfire from an automatic rifle, and you say that it had a significant impact on interethnic relations.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Again, there are two or three questions in one. This murder did happen, the killing of Senad Dervisevic, and I, as police commander, attended the on-site investigation, and it is true that this reservist Boro Grujic killed him with an automatic rifle. The police of Kljuc started the on-site investigation and then it was taken over by CSB Banja Luka. I don't know how it ended, but I know that interethnic relations had already been disturbed, and this killing occurred suddenly. It had all started with a conversation on the high streets. This man was a civilian and the soldier who killed him was a reservist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: They had a quarrel, this reservist of the JNA killed him, you attended the on-site investigation which was then handed over to the army, but after the war the man was tried and convicted?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes. I learned later, after the war, that his trial was taken up again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the murder of Admir Selmanovic in paragraph 73. And because it features in your statement, I suppose it has some impact on interethnic relations.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: At the time, it had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This investigation was headed by a Muslim, Muharem Muheljic?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: First of all, it was an inspector who first came to the site. We have already discussed this and agreed that serious crimes were taken over by the CSB Banja Luka, and they took over this case as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But in this paragraph, in line 6 and 7, you say that the Muslim inspector from Kljuc, Muharem Muheljic, led the investigation, and after the initial investigation nothing happened, no suspects were found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And nothing was done.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting, Your Honour, but Mr. Karadzic said at paragraph 73. It's 43.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must have enunciated poorly. I thought I said 43.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Dzafic. You said the investigation was not completed and no suspects were found. But now you have different information.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I don't have any different information, but I stand behind what I said earlier, that the investigation was continued by the CSB Banja Luka, all the forensic analysis and expertise of weapons, fingerprints, et cetera. I don't know why it says here that this Muhamed Muheljic conducted it. He was the only -- he was the one who came first to the site, but it was taken over later by CSB Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How about this paragraph 43, is it correct in its entirety or are there other corrections to make?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm looking at it in English. I don't understand all of it, but the point is that this Selmanovic man was killed with an automatic weapon, the police in Kljuc was informed first, the on-site investigation began, and early the next morning it was taken over by the CSB Banja Luka. And further investigation led to nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But if we asked the Trial Chamber now, they would be convinced, I'm sure, that this killing is considered to have been committed by the Serbs. But I will read to you from the -- [In English] "The Muslim inspector from Kljuc, Muharem Muheljic, conducted the investigations. After this brief investigation, there was no further investigation and no one was ever arrested. There was never a suspect arrested. The investigation was not thorough, even though there were leads."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, now, could we call up 65 ter 890.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who was a suspect in this case, although you say there were no suspects?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I don't remember such details, really. Although I would very much wish to be of assistance, I can't. It was a long time ago, after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As a policeman, do you know how many murder cases are generally solved by good police forces throughout the world? What is the percentage?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Anything beyond 35, 40 per cent, or up to 50 per cent, is considered to be good in European countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please look at this document from the Ministry of the Interior. Public security station Kljuc. It says serious crimes committed by unidentified perpetrators, and the first paragraph refers to the killing of Admir Selmanovic in a place called Sanica on 27 April 1992, killed by gunfire, six entry and exit wounds on the body, motive unknown. On suspicion that they have committed the crime, Mehmed Karadzic and Fahim Alibegovic were remanded in custody after three days, but, for lack of evidence, the aforementioned were released after this term. Is it normally the case that when more evidence is collected, the case can be taken up again?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: This was very professionally phrased, which does not mean that this Mehmed Karadzic and Alibegovic really committed the murder. But this paragraph was really professionally phrased.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, they were your disciples, so they must have phrased it professionally. Just tell me: Are these Karadzic and Alibegovic Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: You know, this surname Karadzic is so common. I have a nephew by the surname Karadzic. And there was a chief in Jajce, Midhat Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But do we agree that these suspects are both Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, those suspects were Muslims. But look at when this was written, 23rd November 1992, when it was all mono-ethnic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But look at this, sir. This is a response to a query from the ministry, from the centre in Banja Luka, a query concerning serious crimes between 1st January and 20th November.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I agree. I agree. That's correct. It's an overview, a survey. But it doesn't mean that it hasn't been doctored, cooked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, they released these men for lack of evidence. Why would it be doctored?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said "all right" and it hasn't been recorded. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Dzafic, did you want to say something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I said "all right," it was just something that, you know, came out at the end of this exchange, but I said the only thing I had to say, namely that the text was written by a professional policeman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1744. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now take a quick look at D1733. D1733.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And I believe that at the time you were still commander of this station. Here we see a record of this on-site investigation, and I would just like you to confirm for us whether these people were your employees. Now, please take a look at this. On the 28th, in other words on the next day, an on-site investigation was conducted, the victim was Admir Selmanovic, and this investigation was conducted by --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the name of the person who conducted the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, could you please confirm for us that under number 3 we see the name of a Muslim, Muharem Muheljic and under number 5 we have another Muslim, Mirsad Hasanagic?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I don't see the document. I don't have the document before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You do. It's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I don't. I have nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's 1D4289, which is one of the listed documents. It's a minute of on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If it can help, I will read it for you. The investigation was conducted by Botonjic, Dzemal, an investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is a document already admitted. Let him read it and put your question briefly. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, what is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The date on this document is the 28th of April and at the time you were still commander; correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you confirm that you know that this person, Dzemal Botonjic actually went out on site and conducted an on-site investigation and that he was a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do we see under number 3 the name of Muhamir [as interpreted] Muheljic who was also a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, and he's a forensic technician.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And -- thank you -- and under number 5 we have the name of Mirsad Hasanagic, also a Muslim; correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, he should be, judging by his first and last name. But he was a reserve police officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We've already admitted this document. But it shows that the investigation was conducted at the time, and there is a description of what was done, and you confirm this; correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So, Mr. Dzafic, can we agree on the following: This was not attributed to Serbs, there was no cover-up, and there was an ethnically mixed team of investigators who went on site; correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on. Please take a look at paragraph 44, where I'm a bit confused because you say that in February 1992 a company of reservists of the Serbian JNA was stationed at -- on the premises of the Sip company in Kljuc. Now, how are we to understand the Serbian JNA, that those are your words, is that an error? because it was the JNA.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, it says here that this was a work unit in Sipa [phoen] Kljuc. The premises of that plant were some 15 kilometres away from Kljuc. Now, in that area there was a formation unit. Now, whether it was a company or a battalion-strong unit, I don't know, but they were stationed there for a while and exercised, and they had meals at the Laniste work organisation. They had uniforms of the former JNA, but whether they were JNA members or reserve members, I don't know. But in any case, the incident mentioned here involved a reservist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I just needed to clarify the adjective used there, "Serbian JNA." Now, do you recall that among the five JNA soldiers who were killed toward the end of May in Kljuc there were two Yugoslav Albanians who were serving the army at the time?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I've already told you, and I will repeat it: When this incident occurred in Kljuc, there was a column of JNA members. This was on the 27th of May. I was in Sanica at the time. And as I learned later, three soldiers succumbed to the injuries, whereas five were wounded. I don't know the ethnic composition of those soldiers. I don't know, nor did I have occasion to hear, anything about it or see anything that would show it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Okay. But let's just agree on what you've said here. Would you withdraw the "Serbian" from the "Serbian JNA" phrase that you used and leave it at just "JNA"?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, I've been trying to recall the events of the time and in any case my conclusion is that this incident involved reservists of the army. I don't know from which unit, whether it was a company or a battalion, but they were from other municipalities, not from the Kljuc municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But they were a JNA unit; right?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, I really don't know. At this point in time it's hard to judge, and I can't say either way. I don't want to err.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But had it been anything other than the JNA, wouldn't the whole world have resonated of this? Because, remember, what other army could it have been other than the JNA? What other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I would like you to proceed. What significance would it have in terms of your indictment? Come to the issues.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will, Your Excellency, but this long paragraph, 44, is not there by error, and it implies that there was a Serbian army and they -- that their conduct was as described here. And I would appreciate it if your comments were also addressed to the Prosecution, not just to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. It's worth commenting that in the future, in compiling the amalgamated statement, the Prosecution should try to not -- try not to contain peripheral issues, but that's a separate issue. You have less than 25 minutes to conclude.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I have only been able to deal with less than 50 paragraphs. There are 140 here. How do you expect me to complete my examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber allowed you to have two and a half hours with this witness. It is for you how to spend that time allotted to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's precisely -- that's precisely what the issue is. There are so many peripheral issues. And had this statement been more focused, then I wouldn't have had this problem. But I will try to skip over certain matters. But I would just like to say for the record that whatever I do skip, it should not be considered that I did not challenge it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dzafic, please take a look at paragraphs 46 and 47. I won't read them. But this is one of those examples where you have these contradictory orders. Avdo Hebib reported to you that from Slunj in Croatia and other areas where there were combat operations under way there would be a long column of civilians coming through Kljuc and that they should be allowed to move on to Central Bosnia. Now, you received this information, didn't you, but your boss, Vinko Kondic, considered that those people should not be allowed through without any checks, and he actually kept back some 60 or 70 able-bodied men and rounded them up and sent them to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, would you agree with me that with this -- this whole --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please repeat his question, it was unclear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat your last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that in this particular case people were coming from areas where there were combat operations under way, that among them there may have been some Croatian fighters, and that Avdo Hebib actually bypassed both Banja Luka and the second man in Banja Luka where he reported that this column should be allowed through. Now, according to you, was this a highly unusual occurrence, and was this irregular, in fact?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, in principle, yes. But under ordinary circumstances, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, here we see paragraph 48, where the removal of weapons belonging to Territorial Defence is being discussed. And you say that in late 1991 and early 1992 the weapons of the TO were removed from Kljuc to the Kula municipality, and the Muslims protested because they believed that those weapons were going to be sent to Kupres to be used in combat there; correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber, in early April 1992, what fighting, and against whom, was underway at Kupres?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I can't really recall these combat operations in Kupres in the early days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, let me try to refresh your memory. Bosnia-Herzegovina was still part of Yugoslavia. The regular Croatian troops went to Kupres, attacking Serbian villages, and the JNA was defending them; correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, I can only tell you that I did not follow those events and I can't recall what transpired, but if you say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, why, then, in paragraph 48 do you say that the Muslims protested against their weapons being taken to Kupres?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, this may be an error. They protested because the infantry weapons were being removed from Kljuc and moved to the Kula warehouse in Mrkonjic Grad. It was a military depot, the Kula military depot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So paragraph 48 is not completely accurate; correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know why Kupres would be mentioned here. It should read Kula, the warehouse in Kula. That is a reserve depot, military depot, in Kula, towards Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And that was under JNA control; correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that in 1990, before the elections in August, the Presidency of the SFRY, the old communist Presidency, ordered that TO weapons should be placed under JNA control and you failed to do that in Kljuc; correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about such a decision by the Presidency. I heard about it during my last evidence here, but I did hear about Kljuc not complying with that decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know anything about the Green Berets and their existence in some smaller villages in your municipality, like Velagici and similar?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Would you please tell me what you understand Green Berets to mean. Would that mean any Bosniak who was fighting or a soldier who was armed and equipped and uniformed? What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll show you the paragraph in a moment. But in the meantime tell us, please, do you know or did you know of the existence of the Kljuc Sana Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I didn't know anything about the Kljuc Sana Brigade earlier. I only learned about it in Manjaca or after Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, where do you live? What is the street name where you live now?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, in Kljuc -- or, rather, last year I moved to Sanica, and the (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But what was the name of the street where you lived in Kljuc, before you moved?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, it was called Naselje "Sedamnaeste."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you please give us the full name of that street.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Naselje of the 17th Mountain Brigade. "Naselje Sedamnaeste Brdske Brigade."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The glorious brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, the glorious brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think it's necessary that we have the street name on page 105 at lines 9 and 12 and 14. I'm sorry, I would ask for that to be redacted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to know, Mr. Dzafic, this: Was your street, before you moved from Kljuc, was it called the street of the 17th Chivalrous Brigade, and was that a Muslim brigade during this war?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, after Kljuc was liberated, it was normally for the streets to be renamed. The street on which I lived before the war was called the street of M Tito, but after the war it was renamed into Naselje, or neighbourhood, of the 17th Mountain Brigade, the Chivalrous Brigade, from Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you a member of this brigade?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, please take a look at paragraph 50. You're being asked -- you're asked about the Green Berets in Velagici, so I was not the first to ask you about the Green Berets; correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Please keep on going.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So not -- irrespective of whether this is -- this information is correct or not, there was information about Green Berets in Velagici and you had knowledge about it?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: No. I've already told you I learned about it during my evidence. Now, I did not know about the organisation of the Green Berets. I'm not trying to say that there were no able bodied Bosniak men who perhaps managed to obtain illegally some weapons. But that they were organised or that they were Green Berets, I don't have any information to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now paragraph 51 and the Red Berets -- I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Karadzic, for interrupting. Your Honour, I think it's only necessary to redact the street name at line 9 on page 105.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you noticed the arrival of some Red Berets. And in paragraph 52 you say that you believe that their intentions may have been good, that they reinstated order, that they prevented the escalation of conflicts in Kljuc. That was in early May; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were billeted in the secretariat or the staff of Territorial Defence, and a certain number of those Green Berets were placed at the disposal of us in the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And, now, did you conclude that that was the JNA's response to the objections of the conduct of the reservists and do you agree that the Red Berets had been sent as the military police to help you deal with the problems?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: That was true for a while. They did help us a lot. Those people were well-trained, they were good policemen, especially when it came to dealing with the reservists who returned from various front lines and disrupted public peace and order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 54 you speak about the Crisis Staff. And you say that some people were members of the Crisis Staffs ex officio, and you mentioned that that was also the case in the previous system. As a person familiar with the Law on All People's Defence, would you agree that membership in such ad hoc bodies such as Presidencies, Crisis Staffs, and so on and so forth, that membership in such bodies is ex officio?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree that that was true in the previous system.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Up to that moment, those laws were still in effect, they had not been changed; right?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now, you say, in paragraph 58 possibly, that you were informed by a Serb from Sanica that the Serbs had established a Crisis Staff, and he also advised you to advise the Muslims to form their own Crisis Staff. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. That Muslim staff was never established. Later on, myself and Nedeljko Grabez, who is mentioned in here as the president of the staff in Sanica, were able to establish that a Crisis Staff never existed in Sanica, a Crisis Staff that would have been organised by the Muslims there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. For the benefit of the other participants who do not hail from our area, let's be precise. Mr. Grabez was a Serb from Sanica and the president of the Serbian Crisis Staff. He talked to you and he advised you to form your own Crisis Staff, you Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, it was not a piece of advice. It was our informal conversation, because Grabez and I had spent some time working in education. We knew each other very well from there. He just suggested that in passing. We were standing in the street by the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you then conclude that it was his belief that if you had a Crisis Staff it would be easier for you to deal with the problems in Sanica?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what he may have concluded or not. I can't discuss that. I don't have an answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now, in paragraph 62, you talk about the referendum. Do we agree that that was the referendum that took place in late February? Do you agree that the Serbs abstained and that they did not obstruct you to carry out your referendum?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Every referendum, including that one, should have been secured by the police. As far as I can remember, the implementation of the referendum was not riddled with any incidents. More or less all the polling places were covered by police patrols.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, do you agree that the Serbs had informed you in advance that they would not obstruct the referendum?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I don't remember any such thing, I really don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 63 you say that Vinko Kondic signed that he would join the security services centre in Banja Luka. Before then, was the Kljuc Public Security Station tied to the Security Services Centre in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was. When it comes to joining the Banja Luka region, I made my own conclusions on the basis of the fact that he stopped carrying out orders that came from Sarajevo. He joined the Banja Luka centre, and he carried out their orders and acted on their dispatches.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that on the 13th of February and then on 21st and then the 22nd February, and then finally the 18th of March, we agreed that the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina would have its own republic and that the Muslims will have -- would have their own republic and the Croats would have their own republic, according to the so-called Lisbon Agreement, did you know that?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: It was a long time ago. I knew some of the details, but not all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know, and do you agree, that Kljuc as a whole is very deep in the Serbian territory and that it is surrounded by villages with -- and towns with predominantly Serb population, for example Drvar with almost 100 per cent Serb population, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I would say yes, however Kljuc also borders on Sanski Most and Prijedor. And look at those places in light of the 1991 census.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Kljuc in almost all plans, bar for one, where it says that Muslim parts of Sanski Most, Kljuc, and Prijedor would have cantons, in all the other plans and proposals Kljuc was envisaged as a town in the Republika Srpska, the exception is the Dayton -- are the Dayton Accords, which were signed during the time when war developments conditioned that? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I didn't have that concrete information. I now hear it from you. I really didn't know that. Kljuc is where it is. It cannot be moved. And that's very clear, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we have time we are going to show you a series of maps which will demonstrate that Kljuc has always been considered part of the Republika Srpska by the Muslim leaders and the international mediators. The exceptions to that are the first map and the Owen-Stoltenberg map, which envisaged for Kljuc, Sanski Most, and Prijedor to have Muslim cantons. But I don't think we will get there. We will not have the time to do that. And now you're talking about the establishment of the manoeuvre unit, and do you agree with me that that was something that was customary, that had existed even before, and that my cousin from Jajce Midhat Karadzic refused to obey and to send his police officers to become members of that unit; right?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't use the term that you used. I wouldn't say that he refused. Whether he refused or just didn't want to obey, in any case the manoeuvre unit from Jajce did not attend the joint training in Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, would you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Very brief, Your Honour. Hopefully only five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then we'll take a break now for half an hour. And after which, Mr. Karadzic, you will have ten minutes to conclude your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm wondering if the Chamber would consider giving Dr. Karadzic about 45 minutes so that we can finish with this witness and not have to start another one today, and also because I've noticed that in the Zupljanin case the cross-examination was four hours. They don't have time limits there. And maybe the cross-examination was as good as Dr. Karadzic's, maybe it was better, or maybe it was worse, but in any event those lawyers got to ask all the questions that they felt were relevant and necessary. And I think Dr. Karadzic ought to have the same opportunity, particularly considering that the amalgamated statement is even broader than the direct examination in Zupljanin. It doesn't seem fair that he should be restricted to less time than was given in that case. So I hope you could consider using the balance of the day by having him complete his cross-examination and then the re-direct and we can go home at 4.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, the Chamber has been disappointed by the conduct of Mr. Karadzic's cross-examination today, which was not focused on relevant issues. However, given the peculiar circumstances of today, we will accommodate your request on an exceptional basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much on my behalf as well, and thank you for your patience. I'm an amateur, as you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzafic, in paragraph 71 you say that the Serbs were the ones who wanted the patrols to be of a mixed composition, Serb and Muslim. But then you also say that they wanted to see what kind of weapons the Muslims had been provided with.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: What I had in mind were hunting rifles, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Because those mixed patrols or guards that I knew of had only the hunting rifles that were in their legal possession.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My point is different. In paragraph 71 you say: [In English] "There were demands by the Serbs that there be patrols in the mixed Muslim-Serb villages and that these patrols should be mixed. The Serbs only did this to see what kind of weapons the Muslims had." [Interpretation] Later on, you say that Muslim delegates in Kljuc municipality were against that because they did not want the Serbs to see what Muslims had; right?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: No. On the contrary. Both sides were in favour of mixed patrols. However, I received subsequent information, which was then included in the statement, that the mixed patrols were short-lived. They only lasted for a couple of months. And, indeed, that they just wanted to know what weapons Muslims had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then the Muslim delegates didn't want the Serbs to know that.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know what other people may have been thinking.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Why did Muslims or Muslim delegates speak against mixed patrols?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Where do you read that? I can't find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It is in paragraph 71. [In English] "The Muslim delegates at the Kljuc assembly meetings required that the Serb military and the military police do not go into Muslim areas and that arrests should be only done by the civilian police. The Serbs did not want --" and so and so on.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: This is something completely different, and I adhere by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's go on. In paragraph 73 you say that you were in aware that in Velagici, Pudin Han, the villages had started organising night guard duties, and then you say that they felt that they should organise those patrols because there had been shootings, and so on and so forth. How did you know what they felt?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, the term "feel" may not be appropriate here. I had information, I was privy to the fact that there were shootings, there were fire -- shots fired in those villages into religious buildings and the homes of the veterans, and then the assembly members wanted to install their own guards and patrols in those non-Serb settlements in order to prevent any such activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have a single piece of evidence, a single document, resulting from any investigations about shots being fired into churches and other religious facilities?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I believe that shots were fired in Velagici and Sanica, in the mosques there, or, rather, in their spires. And investigations actually were not carried out, but we had information to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say that on the 2nd of April, 1992, there were legal forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and you said that when you're talking about Bosanska Krupa. What did you have in mind? What kind of legal forces did Bosnia-Herzegovina have on the 2nd of April?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I don't have an answer to that, believe me. I have the translation here to read it a little bit, to remind myself of what is there, but right now I really don't have an answer for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And then in paragraph 75 you say that the police forces started to be formed on a single-ethnic basis. Is it true, Mr. Dzafic, that they were so because you didn't want to work anymore?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, there are a number of questions here. In those circumstances, and the way I explained it, I wasn't able to work any more, and I was removed from my job. I didn't say that I didn't want to work, and I didn't give a statement to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you recall that in May two young Muslims from Sarajevo were sent in May to Kljuc and they were deployed there as young policemen and then later they were permanently employed?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I would like to know their first and last names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Adnan Temimovic; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Adnan Temimovic was a cadet, an active policeman, who worked at the Kljuc Police Station much before the events of the 7th of May, and then he was transferred to the Sanica Police Department and he worked as a policeman there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's look at 22074 or -5. Look at Adamovic. This is page 123. Kondic asked you if, in early May --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this is ERN number -- actually English page 126, Serbian 123, and the ERN number is 061-7021 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: He asked you whether they, after completing the MUP school, they came to Kljuc, and he gave them a job, and they got permanent employment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't have the translation of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You have the Serbian version. You have it there. You have the Serbian variant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Court Deputy should have the transcript in Adamovic trial. 22075, which we saw earlier. Does the witness have it in front of him? Mr. Dzafic, do you have it in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Serbian version is good. And the English version, it should be on page 126. The ERN number is 0671-7021.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "I'm asking you about the beginning of May 1992," both pages are okay?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a minute. The witness is not able to follow the e-court. I'm asking him whether he has it before him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Can you look at it. It says, Accused Kondic, the fifth line from the top, Kosovic [phoen], Kondic, Dzafic, Kondic. I'm asking you about the beginning of May. Is it true that they were employed in May? There is a name here, Adnan Temimovic; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was employed at the time, full time, but he actually was employed much before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But in this transcript you confirm that this was in early May.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I know that this Mr. Temimovic was part of the manoeuvring contingent training at Manjaca, and this was much earlier, before May. He was a staff member. At the beginning of May he was just transferred from Kljuc to Sanica, to the same organisational unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you, Mr. Dzafic, when they finish do they have a certain term of employment and then after that they have to have a period of traineeship and then are permanently employed?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And is that why you think he worked for longer, actually?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't have a specific answer to that, but I know that his employment was for a longer period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you look at paragraph 80 of your statement now. During those two weeks that you were given to consider, you met Omer Filipovic, you considered what to do, should you sign the oath or not; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: On two or three occasions I just happened to get in touch with Mr. Filipovic in order to surmount the newly created situation and to avoid bloodshed, and there was talk even that the loyalty oath should be signed for the Serbian authorities and for us to continue working.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In that paragraph you confirm that you were aware that you knew that the Serbs and Muslims were negotiating the division of Kljuc into a Serbian and Muslim territory; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't know that. I didn't know anything about any division.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But it states here that you found out later that --

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Maybe later I found out. But at that time I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And let's look for just a minute to see if it's correct, to see what was the conclusion regarding the distribution of weapons. The fact that you saw these people, did that have anything to do with the preparation of fighting and the distribution of weapons?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, look, there are a few questions there. I did say that I saw and spoke with Mr. Filipovic several times only in reference to the signing. As to the other activities, distribution of weapons, shipments, combat activities, we did not -- actually, nobody talked to me about any of those topics, not even once.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at D1352 just for a minute, please. D1352. And if we can have page 17, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you carry out training of extremists and concealed their actions, actions of policemen who took part in that?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: No. Had I done that, Mr. Karadzic, I wouldn't be sitting here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, can you look at item 7. In July 1992, before you were released, this is what the Serbs thought, and they received information that this is what you were doing. Look, operative work established that a number of the SJB --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 17 can we have in the English -- [In English] Point 7, point 7. Next, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you can see; I don't have to read it out to you. Can you see this?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Page 17?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 7, the involvement of police employees in the legal distribution of weapons and training of extremists. And it states here that they took part in the capture of seven soldiers from Crljin to Krasulje, and together with Atif Dzafic they all trained extremists and concealed their activities. There is still operative work underway for certain former SJB employees. And this was all received from Alija Bilip or Bilic. He's a retired employee.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I state that the activities that are mentioned in this last sentence, that I carried out training of extremists and concealed their actions, that's what it says here. Anything can be written anywhere. But there is no evidence of me having committed any of these activities. And had I done anything of that, I wouldn't have even reached Manjaca. And, you know, as a person who experienced all the things that I experienced, I do not wish to insult anyone or underestimate anyone. I mean, you insulted me in our previous conversation. But with dignity, with full responsibility, and in the material sense, I say that what I'm saying is true. Anything can be written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You can be sure that I have no intention of insulting you. I'm just trying to establish the truth. Do you know that seven soldiers were captured at Crljin?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I found that out later, about how many were captured. I didn't take part in that. And there is no point in you putting questions to me about that. I've already said where I was and what I was doing in that period. What I know is what I'm telling you, and that is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In -- according to what you know, did this Atif Dedic participate in the capture of those policemen?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, Atif Dedic was a policeman. That's what it says here. I don't know whether he took part in that or not. You should ask him that. And the other soldiers who, as far as I know, attacked a Muslim village, of the village of Crljin, this is something that should be looked at from several aspects, and the truth should be established.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzafic, I have to ask you, without any intention to insult you, Are you saying that the soldiers attacked the village and were captured or they were captured without any kind of attack having taken place while they were in a column? Just tell me what you are asserting, and then we'll see later.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, let's be clear. I don't know. Perhaps we're not thinking of the same thing, of the same period, the same date, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you look at paragraph 90 of your statement, where you say that you heard in Manjaca that Atif Dedic, Muslim policeman, was one of the people who captured seven Serbian soldiers.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear that in Manjaca. But later you can read what it says in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And is it correct that he was dismissed from the police after that?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, no. This happened at the time when we were dismissed from the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And those five soldiers who were killed, the JNA soldiers, of the JNA that was withdrawing, were not five soldiers killed in the column that was withdrawing from Knin to Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, this case is just one case that you're asking me about, regarding Atif Dedic. And this other thing is another incident. As far as I know, according to some information, three or five were killed in the column. That is correct. And these ones here, five -- or, rather, seven, were captured in the Bosniak settlement of Crljin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And is it correct that on the 27th of May a synchronised number of attacks were executed against the Serbian soldiers and army in the Kljuc municipality?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I have no answer to that question. I wasn't really informed about it because already on the 21st or the 22nd I was in Sanica, which is my birthplace, and this actually happened on the 27th of May. And I would like to ask you to actually dwell on this as little as possible, questions like this, where I was not an eyewitness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you write about that in your statement. In 82, you say that you went to Sanica and that you heard that there would be shelling. Isn't it correct that Sanica was never shelled?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, the shelling of Sanica was announced. It was announced.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But it didn't actually happen; right?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: No, not in Sanica, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you say that some of us escaped to the forest. We hid in the forest. Who hid in the forest?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: When the shelling was announced, the shelling of the Sanica area, all the inhabitants, women, children, of course all the adults, fled to the nearby woods, and I was also in one of those columns of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When was this exactly?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but it was in the period from the 22nd to the 26th. Excuse me, I don't know exactly. It was from the 22nd, thereabouts, up until the 30th of May. I cannot recall the exact date, but I know that with my family, with my elderly mother, and the others, we escaped.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you talk about the 1st of June in paragraph 84 and you speak about civilians, what are civilians to you, Mr. Dzafic? Is it that they are wearing civilian clothing? And is a policeman and a fighter still that when they change into civilian clothing, or do they turn into civilians?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, it's well known what a civilian is and what a uniformed person is. A soldier, a policeman, wearing a uniform. Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And was it a widespread occurrence in Bosnia that people, at least during the first year, actually fought wearing civilian clothing?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, where I was, after being dismissed from the police, in that period, there was nobody fighting in civilian clothing. Actually neither in civilian clothing, neither in uniform. That's where I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, Your Honour, but I would ask Mr. Karadzic not to misquote the evidence. He says, in page 120, line 17 to 19: "And is it correct that on the 27th of May a synchronised number of attacks were executed against the Serbian soldiers and army in the Kljuc municipality?" And then the witness goes on to say: "I have no answer to that question." I wasn't informed about this, and goes on. And then Mr. Karadzic says: "But you write about that in your statement," in paragraph 82. And then goes on to say: "... you say that you went to Sanica and that you heard that there would be shelling. Isn't it correct ..." And that's not -- none of that is contained in paragraph 82.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. Thank you, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in paragraph 82, and I have to read now, there it is, 82: [In English] [As read] "I could hear the sound of gunfire and in and around the village of Pudin Han and Velagici and that what sounded like artillery fire and exploding shells. Also during that time I saw five or six houses were ..." and so on. [Interpretation] Or perhaps it's 83. But the witness confirmed it. I don't have to call up the document if the witness confirms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzafic, you mention in paragraph 85 the time when you were detained in the gym of the school in Sanica. You say that Milan Tomic told you that the investigative team was late because the Green Berets had set an ambush at Biljani, on the road from Kljuc to Sanica which was blocked.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: That's Tomic's evidence. He told not only me but all of us who were detained there, who had been illegally, unlawfully, brought to that gym, but we only laughed at it because we knew that neither was the road blocked at Biljani, nor were there any Green Berets to set ambushes. That's what he said, his words.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How could you, sitting in that gym, know that it's not true, while he, with a hand-held radio and contact with the police station, doesn't know?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: We knew it wasn't true because it was not in the Bosniaks' interest to do anything like that. They wouldn't care to do something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you reckoned they wouldn't do something like that and on that basis you say there was no roadblock and no ambush by the Green Berets. Do you have any stronger argument to support what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: At that time, I had some information, and that's why we laughed when he said that. If there had been any Green Berets in the area of Biljani, we would have known about it, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your evidence in the Adamovic case, 22075, page 10, you say that the head of department, Milan Tomic, said we should be patient. Wait for a while. A team of investigators from Kljuc would come, question us, and of course, those who are found to be innocent will be released to go home, and those who are found to be responsible would be held accountable. Is that what he said?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And when the investigators were running late, he explained that it was because of an ambush in Biljani.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, those were his words.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that some people were killed at Biljani. Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I did not see that, nor was I able to see that. On 10 July, when that happened in Biljani, I was at Manjaca, and I didn't even mention it anywhere. I just learned in 1996, during the exhumation of mass graves, that all the people from the Biljani area were exhumed from Laniste 1 site, 189 persons. I attended the exhumation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know how they died?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: How they met their death? I learned later that they had been brought in, put on two buses to go to Manjaca, but they never arrived at Manjaca. They ended up at Laniste where they were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's what you heard from someone and you have no other knowledge about it?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: No. No. After the war I was appointed chief of the police administration in Kljuc, and as chief of that administration it was my duty to attend the exhumations. I had opportunity to see all sorts of documents and statements. I was not an eyewitness in that case except attending the exhumation of mass graves, and I believe there are witnesses who were eye witnesses and who can confirm this better than I can. But I do know that whole bodies were recovered from that grave, bodies that were not damaged, and they -- it was clear that they had been shot with a bullet to the head.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you do say that only a survivor could really confirm what happened.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes. A survivor could testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then a survivor is suddenly found and comes here to testify.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that. It's not my decision, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have misled the parties. It's in paragraph 88, in fact, you told the investigator, Vasic, that Sanica would be shelled, as you had heard, and you would go to hide in the woods. Vasic, in fact, asked you why you were going to hide in the woods and you answered that you had heard Sanica would be shelled. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: When I was being brought to the gym in that school, of course I was questioned, among others by Vasic, and he made some sort of official note, and I told him all I knew. Nothing else. And among other things I told him that when I heard about the shelling I went with my entire family and some other neighbours to the woods. We didn't stay there for a long time, for an hour or two at most, and as soon as it got dark, we went home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 91 you say you were questioned as to why you had killed your assistant Dusan Stojakovic.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: You are insulting me. Nobody asked me why I had killed him. They questioned me as to what I knew about who might have killed him. Stojakovic had been my colleague for years. I was not there when he was killed and I told you many times I wasn't there. And I don't know under what circumstances he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzafic, I am not accusing you of anything. But you say in paragraph 91 that you were questioned about that, about his death. [In English] "He asked me why I killed Stojakovic and why I did not come to his funeral." [Interpretation] That's written in paragraph 91 of your statement, and I'm not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you read the next sentence as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "I told him that I did not kill him and that I was in Sanica and that I could not come to the funeral because it was in Ribnik, 25 kilometres," and so on. I'm not asking you here whether you killed him. I'm asking you whether they asked you that, whether you were a suspect. I'm interested in the grounds for your arrest, and that you hid in the forest, that you trained terrorists, that you covered up illegal activities of the policemen involving weapons. All these are circumstances I want to shed light on.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: That's what you're saying, Mr. Karadzic. But I can answer each of these questions, and I have answered them already. I told you nicely where I actually was. And I'm warning you, and I'm telling the Trial Chamber as well, that if it had been noted -- if I had been seen hiding in those woods, and if I had been caught training anyone, let alone terrorists, I would not be sitting here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm not interested in that. I'm interested in why you were treated as a suspect. What was the reason for your arrest? And did they really ask you why you had killed Stojakovic, as written in paragraph 91?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, they had to ask me as well as all the others. There was no reason to arrest me. There was no reason for all the beatings and the abuse and all that was done to me. If there had been any real evidence of anything, they wouldn't talk to me at all. They just thought that I, as police commander, perhaps had more information than others. And that's why they put those questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that material evidence had some importance for the Serbs? Isn't that what you said a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Of course. Everyone is looking for proof.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At Manjaca, you were --

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I was on duty at the barn.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in paragraph 105 you say every morning you toured the place, asking if anybody needed a physician.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: In that barn, where after the first 10 days I was named commander of barn number 2, which held on average 600 to 800 prisoners, my job was to check every morning if any of the prisoners needed to have their wounds bandaged, needed medicine or anything. Such prisoners would be taken to the adjacent building to be examined.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In every barn, were the monitors on duty the most prominent people among the prisoners? Omer was on duty in another barn.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Omer was not a monitor of any kind. He was in the third barn. Whether they were really the most prominent or well-respected people, I don't know. For instance, one man I know, who was initially appointed monitor, was unable to do that job so he was replaced.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did those people, who wanted to volunteer to go out to work, report to you or someone else?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, there were several problems with that. One of them was that every morning a certain number of prisoners had to be sent out to work. Sometimes it was necessary to choose a hundred or even more prisoners very quickly, and there were not enough volunteers. And towards the end there were no volunteers at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How many Muslims lived in the whole of Kljuc municipality?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: You mean before the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Around 17.000; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: 17.000; right. 47.something Serbs and 49.something Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 111, you say that there were 60 to 70 in every hall. How many halls existed there at all?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: That's a mistake. From the area of Kljuc, on the original list, Mr. Karadzic, only from the area of Kljuc, 1.163 prisoners from Kljuc turned over, and that's not even counting the minors and the elderly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: From the area of Kljuc, with a population of 17.000?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, tell me, you have confirmed that in 1995, when you arrived, Serbs had fled Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is Kljuc municipality now divided between Serbs and Muslims; so Serbs have the area facing Ribnik and the Muslims have the area facing Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well the Dayton Accords divided Kljuc municipality into two parts. Exactly as you described. The area with the majority Serb population went to the Republika Srpska, and the remaining part to the federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzafic, wouldn't it have been better if that had been accomplished by the Lisbon agreement without war, than the Dayton Accords after the war?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it was not my decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the incident in Velagici. Do you know that that incident has been investigated and that people were tried?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. But concerning the incident in Velagici, I can repeat the following: While I was in Manjaca, a while into my detention, one night two or three prisoners came to my barn and one of them was from Velagici, Kljuc municipality. His name was Suad Draganovic. He was trembling with fear, beaten up, black and blue, and he told me the story of what happened at Velagici. Now, whether anyone was held responsible, whether anyone was tried or convicted, I don't know. But the bodies of those people from Velagici were found eventually in the mass grave of Laniste 2, 79 of them, whole bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it's almost time to conclude.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Just two questions, to finish this one and another.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Serbian authorities, or, rather, Republika Srpska, treated that as a crime, and judgements were made in that case?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about it. In fact, I don't know any details. I wouldn't go into that discussion. But it's only natural, it's only to be expected, that the perpetrators should be tried and punished.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you also mentioned the incident in Biljani on 10th of July, and you say in paragraph 140 that some tried to escape, around 20 were killed. And then you say around 270 people, or, rather, men, women, and children, who had been in that collective centre were killed. Do you know that for a fact, how those people were killed? I mean, apart from those who had tried to escape?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I don't know the details. I wasn't there. Let's get that clear. From what I know and from what I saw in the mass grave of Laniste 1, bodies were buried in two layers, and those were residents of Biljani. And among them was a three-month-old baby girl. I was there during that exhumation. And of course there were corpses of women and elderly men. And the logical inference from that number of victims is that's how they died. But I didn't investigate it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say that only men were incarcerated in Sanica. You say that in your paragraph 147; right?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: In the sports hall in Sanica. Only men were incarcerated. And among them there were also minors. And there were also people who were over 65 years of age at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you say in your paragraph 150 that in those prisons, you believe that nobody was killed there.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: No. Nobody was killed in Sanica while I was there. In Kljuc, where I was also incarcerated in a sports hall, while I was there for that one day and the night, or perhaps even longer, nobody was killed while I was there. In Sitnica, where I spent about seven days in a sports hall, I'm not aware of anybody having been killed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And just one more question. You say that there was no health care in those detention centres. However, in your last paragraph you say that you were kept for 24 hours in Sanica and some other places for one or two days; right?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes. I spent about 24 hours in Sanica. There was no food, there was no medical attention. People were asked for drugs or help but nothing was forthcoming.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you're talking about the 24 hours that you were there?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dzafic. Please do not think that I tried to attack you in any way. I just wanted to find out how come that 1700 out of 17.000 Muslims in Kljuc were interrogated and incarcerated.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I apologise. 1.630 were in Manjaca alone. And there were other camps and other prisons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
